description: Companion to trials.json: notable ME/CFS research papers (pathomechanism, biomarkers, drug targets, treatment/trial results, genetics), prioritising Wirth/Scheibenbogen but NOT Germany-restricted. Seeded 2026-06-26 with a one-time comprehensive backfill of landmark + recent work (each verified via DOI/PubMed); routine runs add newer papers going forward. Shown on the dashboard's Papers tab. STYLE: write 'summary' and 'why' for a layperson — plain language, short sentences, jargon only where unavoidable and explained in a few words. Confirm each via DOI/journal/preprint before recording; never fabricate.

papers.title: Registered interventional trials fail to cover patient-prioritised treatments in Post-COVID condition (PCC)
papers.authors: Gabriel M, Koster S, Puta C, Katzer K, Reuken PA, Stallmach A
papers.summary: Researchers compared 714 registered post-COVID studies (from ClinicalTrials.gov, the German registry DRKS, and the EU registry) against a list of 29 treatments that patients and their doctors say they actually rely on day to day. Only about 1 in 14 of those studies tested any of those patient-favoured treatments. Post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity that is the hallmark of ME/CFS) was assessed at all in 57 trials, but was the main thing being measured in only 8 of them. Ten common treatment types — for nervous-system regulation problems, allergic-type mast-cell reactions, and certain repurposed nerve drugs — had no registered trial anywhere, and Germany's DRKS registry had zero trials matching any patient-priority treatment.
papers.why: Backs up, with hard numbers, a pattern this tracker keeps finding: solid drug trials aimed at the ME/CFS-like PEM symptom are rare, especially in Germany. It makes a data-driven case for steering funding — including Germany's new decade-long "Nationale Dekade" research programme — toward the treatments patients and doctors already believe help, rather than only mechanism-focused studies.
papers.notes: Jena University Hospital group (Gabriel/Puta/Katzer/Reuken/Stallmach). Meta-research/landscape-analysis preprint, not new patient biology: deduplicated 854 registry records (ClinicalTrials.gov, DRKS, EU-CTR; snapshot 16 Jul 2026) into 714 unique interventional PCC trials, cross-referenced against 29 patient-guide treatments; 51/714 (7.1%) covered any guide treatment, 20 active; PEM captured in 57 trials but co-primary endpoint in only 8; 10 guide treatments (autonomic-dysfunction first-line agents, mast-cell stabilisers, several repurposed neuromodulators) had zero registered trials; DRKS contributed no guide-relevant trial. Directly relevant context for this tracker's own difficulty finding PEM-targeted German drug trials. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/date/DOI match) and Research Square publisher-page DOI resolution.

papers.title: A Multivariable Plasma Extracellular Vesicle Surface Profile Associated with Post-COVID-19 Syndrome
papers.authors: Erhart DK, Ressin H, Balz LT, Chatterjee S, Lule D, Mueller S, Lewerenz J, Muench J, Tumani H, Gross RM
papers.summary: Blood and spinal-fluid samples from 61 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms, 80 fully recovered people, and 10 people with fatigue after other infections were tested for extracellular vesicles (EVs) — tiny particles cells release into the blood, a bit like sealed messages — looking at proteins on their surface. No single surface protein reliably told the groups apart on its own, but a computer model combining small differences across many proteins together could distinguish post-COVID patients from recovered people reasonably well, and this combined "EV score" dropped back down a year later in patients who improved.
papers.why: Adds a new type of candidate blood test for post-COVID syndrome — based on particles cells shed, rather than antibodies or hormones — from the same Ulm University team already tracked here for finding no unusual brain immune activity in these patients. Together, the two findings point research away from classic autoimmune brain inflammation and toward other biology (e.g. how cells communicate) as a driver of lasting symptoms.
papers.notes: Posted medRxiv Aug 31, 2026. Ulm University group (Erhart, Balz, Lule, Muench, Lewerenz, Tumani — same team as the already-tracked erhart-2026-cns-immune-activation-postcovid paper; likely overlapping cohort/companion analysis). n=61 post-COVID syndrome (COVIDpost) vs 80 recovered (COVIDreco) vs 10 non-SARS-CoV-2 post-viral syndrome; bead-based multiplex flow cytometry of 37 tetraspanin- and phosphatidylserine-directed EV surface markers in plasma and CSF; no single marker survived FDR correction, but an L1-regularised logistic-regression classifier under nested cross-validation achieved AUC 0.788 (plasma tetraspanin panel); EV classification score declined at 1-year follow-up in improving patients. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed — confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record and medRxiv DOI resolution.

papers.title: Plasma Proteomics Identifies a Microtesla Magnetic Therapy Response Signature in Long COVID
papers.authors: Brady NR, Canori A, Maltz D, Kirsher DY, Zhou W, Becker J, Putrino DF, Gurfein BT
papers.summary: In a small trial of a gentle, at-home, whole-brain magnetic-field treatment ("Microtesla Magnetic Therapy") for long-COVID brain fog, some treated patients' thinking and symptoms improved. Researchers then measured over 11,000 blood proteins before and after treatment and found a pattern of about 17 proteins that changed specifically in people who got better, including one protein that normally puts the brakes on a cell-signalling pathway (called Hedgehog signalling) tied to inflammation and tissue repair — suggesting the treatment may work partly by calming inflammation.
papers.why: Offers early molecular evidence that a non-drug, brain-stimulation approach can produce a measurable biological change in long COVID, and flags specific blood proteins that could help predict who will respond to this or similar treatments — though this is a small feasibility study, not a definitive trial.
papers.notes: Posted medRxiv Aug 27, 2026 (indexed ~Aug 31). Mount Sinai / Cortene collaboration (senior author David Putrino, a prominent long-COVID researcher; Gurfein lab). Randomised, sham-controlled feasibility trial of at-home Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT, low-amplitude whole-brain RF electromagnetic field) for long-COVID cognitive impairment; SomaScan 11K plasma proteomics on paired baseline/week-4 samples, post-hoc responder classification; 17-protein exploratory response signature, top hit Hedgehog interacting protein (HHIP), pathway analysis consistent with reduced inflammatory/injury signalling. No German site/sponsor (US-based) — tracked on papers side only per ROUTINE.md (papers not Germany-restricted). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed — confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record and medRxiv DOI resolution.

papers.title: eNOS Uncoupling, Shear-Stress Tolerance, and the Two-Threshold Model of Post-Exertional Malaise in Long COVID: A Mechanistic Hypothesis With Implications for Physiotherapy and Recovery Protocols
papers.authors: Karipidis YK, Karipidis KY
papers.summary: This paper is a theory piece (not a study with new patients) about post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity) in some long-COVID patients whose blood vessels look normal on standard scans. The authors propose that COVID-19 damages the inner lining of blood vessels in a way that uses up a helper molecule the body needs to make nitric oxide, a gas that normally helps blood vessels relax and handle the extra blood flow during activity. Without enough of that helper molecule, the same machinery that should make nitric oxide instead makes harmful byproducts, which the authors think build up during and after exertion and trigger the crash.
papers.why: Offers a specific, testable blood-vessel-based explanation for PEM, different from the muscle-calcium theory (Klaus Wirth's hypothesis) or nervous-system theories already tracked here, and suggests concrete before/after-exercise blood tests that could check whether it's right. It also suggests too much rest, not only too much activity, could worsen blood-vessel function — relevant to how patients are advised to pace themselves.
papers.notes: Microcirculation (New York, N.Y.) 33(6):e70082, published Aug 1, 2026. Two authors, one listed as an independent researcher — a hypothesis/review paper, not new patient data, published in a legitimate peer-reviewed vascular-biology journal (Wiley). Framed around Long COVID specifically rather than ME/CFS by name, but explicitly addresses post-exertional malaise (PEM), which is in scope per ROUTINE.md's post-infectious ME/CFS inclusion. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed independently via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Acupressure and Qigong in post-infectious fatigue with impaired physical function: a randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Dietzel J, Bauer T, Tissen-Diabaté T, Ortiz M, Siewert J, Bellmann-Strobl J, Engelhardt U, Roll S, Grabowska W, Scheibenbogen C, Willich SN, Paul F, Brinkhaus B
papers.summary: In this Charité-led trial ('ACUQiG'), 235 people with lasting fatigue and reduced physical functioning after an infection (mostly post-COVID) were split into two groups: one did 8 weeks of daily self-applied acupressure (pressing on specific body points, about 18 minutes a day) plus twice-weekly online Qigong (a gentle mind-body exercise), while the other just got a self-care information leaflet. On the main measure — physical functioning — the acupressure/Qigong group scored a bit higher after 8 weeks, but the difference was too small to be statistically certain it wasn't due to chance. A separate fatigue scale did show a small, statistically real improvement in the treatment group.
papers.why: A rigorously tested complementary-medicine approach, run by Carmen Scheibenbogen's own Charité group, came back essentially negative on its main goal of restoring physical function — useful, honest evidence for tempering expectations about this kind of non-drug approach, even though it showed a small effect on fatigue specifically.
papers.notes: Frontiers in Medicine, vol. 13, published online Aug 10, 2026. Charité (Institute for Social Medicine, Epidemiology and Health Economics — Brinkhaus/Roll group — with Scheibenbogen and Bellmann-Strobl from the Fatigue Centrum as co-authors). RCT 'ACUQiG', n=235 (118 intervention / 117 control) with post-infectious/post-COVID fatigue and impaired physical function, 85% female, mean age 42; 8 weeks of self-applied acupressure (9 mandatory + up to 2 symptom-specific points) plus twice-weekly online Qigong vs. self-care leaflet only (both arms received written complementary-medicine guidance). Primary outcome (SF-36 Physical Functioning Subscale at 8 weeks): intervention 55.4 vs control 51.2, adjusted mean difference 4.2 (95% CI -0.9 to 9.4, p=0.109) — not statistically significant. Responder analysis (>=10-point improvement) favored intervention (58.9% vs 46.3%, OR 1.69, p=0.058) but also not significant. Chalder Fatigue Scale showed a small but statistically significant improvement (21.4 vs 23.2, p=0.040). Adherence 76.8% (acupressure) / 62.5% (Qigong). HIGH PRIORITY (Scheibenbogen-affiliated). Confirmed via Frontiers publisher page (frontiersin.org, abstract/results) and Europe PMC core record (author list/journal/date match).

papers.title: Central noradrenergic deficiency in post-infectious chronic fatigue: neurobehavioral correlates
papers.authors: Aregawi L, Walitt B, Sullivan P, Norato G, Benjamin RN, Goldstein DS
papers.summary: Researchers at the US National Institutes of Health tested spinal fluid from 16 people with ME/CFS, 34 with long COVID, 32 with Parkinson's disease (included for comparison, since it's a known noradrenaline-system disease), and 40 healthy volunteers, looking at two brain chemical messengers: noradrenaline (which drives alertness and the body's 'fight or flight' response) and dopamine. People with ME/CFS had clearly lower noradrenaline activity than healthy people — even lower than the long-COVID and Parkinson's groups — while their dopamine levels were normal. This noradrenaline shortfall was linked to weaker hand-grip endurance, worse general health, and was even lower in those who experience post-exertional malaise (PEM, a crash after activity).
papers.why: Identifies a specific, measurable brain-chemical shortfall in ME/CFS, distinct from a general 'stress' response, and ties it directly to muscle fatigability and symptom severity. The authors suggest it may happen because making noradrenaline costs cells more energy than an ME/CFS-affected 'energy crisis' can supply — offering a concrete, testable mechanism and a possible new drug target (boosting noradrenaline signalling).
papers.notes: Brain Communications 8(3):fcag173 (PMID 42205163, PMCID PMC13202209), published online May 13, 2026; newly surfaced via a Health Rising discussion piece on Aug 27, 2026, hence flagged in this run despite being a few months old. NIH Intramural group (Walitt is part of the Nath/Hallett ME/CFS deep-phenotyping collaborators already tracked via walitt-2024-nih-deep-phenotyping and bedard-2026-central-fatigability-neuroimaging). Measured CSF catecholamine (norepinephrine/dopamine) pathway activity: ME/CFS n=16, long COVID n=34, Parkinson's disease n=32 (positive control), healthy volunteers n=40. Norepinephrine pathway activity markedly reduced in ME/CFS (p=0.00055) and to a lesser extent in long COVID (p=0.05) and Parkinson's, while dopamine pathway activity was normal in both post-infectious groups; reduced norepinephrine activity correlated with worse handgrip-strength maintenance and lower general health, more pronounced in those with PEM. Authors hypothesize inadequate cellular ATP impairs the energy-intensive resynthesis of norepinephrine via VMAT2. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API core record (full metadata, abstract, PMID/PMCID).

papers.title: Neuroendocrine signature of ME/CFS: Meta-analytic evidence for bioactive cortisol deficit and exaggerated feedback sensitivity
papers.authors: Woo TW, Choi YJ, Kim JY, Lee JS, Son CG
papers.summary: The body's main stress hormone, cortisol, is made and controlled by a chain of glands called the HPA axis (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis). Pooling 46 earlier studies (about 1,400 ME/CFS patients vs 1,350 healthy people), researchers found ME/CFS patients consistently have lower cortisol in their saliva, urine and hair, respond more weakly when given a hormone that should trigger a cortisol surge, and suppress their cortisol too strongly when given a steroid that should dampen it slightly.
papers.why: Points to a genuinely blunted, over-braked stress-hormone system in ME/CFS — not just 'stress' in the everyday sense — that could help explain the poor sleep, brain fog, and low resilience to physical or emotional strain patients report, and gives researchers a measurable target (cortisol testing) to explore for future treatments.
papers.notes: Molecular Psychiatry 31(9):5172-5183, published online 2026-04-23. Daejeon University (Research Center for ME/CFS), South Korea group — not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated, but bears on general ME/CFS pathomechanism/biomarkers (HPA-axis dysfunction). Meta-analysis of 46 case-control studies, n=1,388 ME/CFS vs 1,349 controls; lower salivary/urinary/hair cortisol, blunted ACTH-stimulation response, exaggerated dexamethasone-suppression feedback — interpreted as a hyporeactive HPA axis. Slightly outside the routine's usual ~3-month recency window (published Apr 2026, found via this run's fresh open-ended sweep) but flagged as a substantial, high-impact meta-analysis not previously in the tracker, on the same precedent as other slightly-older high-relevance papers added in prior runs (e.g. the Nature Communications skeletal-muscle paper). Confirmed independently via Europe PMC REST API core record (title/authors/journal/volume/issue/pages/DOI/abstract match); Nature.com publisher page itself is paywalled/login-gated for direct fetch.

papers.title: REenergizeME: intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia treatment for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome — protocol for a randomised, placebo-controlled trial
papers.authors: Nochi M, Kristensen SK, Mehrani N, Guerreiro I, Nørholm IMD, Chandra S, Olufsen M, Gudbergsen LR, Brinth LS, Stokholm R, Karlsson P, Tankisi H, Mehlsen J, Foldager CB, Olsen RKJ
papers.summary: This is a study plan (a protocol, not results yet) for a trial testing 'intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia treatment' (IHHT) — repeated short cycles of breathing air with less, then more, oxygen than normal — meant to retrain the body's energy-making machinery in 104 adults with ME/CFS in Denmark.
papers.why: Tests a non-drug approach aimed at a specific proposed cause of ME/CFS fatigue — cells struggling to handle oxygen and produce energy properly — with quality of life and post-exertional malaise (a crash after activity) as key outcomes; worth watching for when results are published, though this paper reports no outcomes yet.
papers.notes: BMJ Open 16(8):e117729, published online 2026-08-14 (PMID 42601095). Aarhus University, Denmark — not a German sponsor/site (tracked on papers side only; papers are not Germany-restricted per ROUTINE.md). Protocol only, n=104 planned, randomised placebo-controlled trial of intermittent hypoxia-hyperoxia treatment (IHHT) in ME/CFS meeting International Consensus Criteria; primary outcome quality of life, secondary outcomes incl. PEM severity. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (title/authors/journal/DOI match).

papers.title: Facility-Measured Sleep Electroencephalographic Microstructures in Long COVID
papers.authors: Sun H, Dang R, Li P, Xiao W, Scott-Sutherland J, Sassower KC, Westover MB, Felsenstein D, Thomas RJ, Haack M, Mullington JM
papers.summary: Overnight brain-wave recordings (sleep EEG) compared 28 people with long COVID, 19 with ME/CFS, and 28 healthy people. Both patient groups showed unusual patterns in the fine details of their sleep brain waves, but ME/CFS patients had some extra abnormalities — like disconnected slow 'sleep spindles' — not seen in long COVID, suggesting the two illnesses disturb sleep in overlapping but not identical ways.
papers.why: Offers a measurable, objective marker for the poor, unrefreshing sleep that ME/CFS and long-COVID patients commonly report, and hints that ME/CFS may involve extra sleep disruption beyond what's seen in long COVID.
papers.notes: Sleep 49(8):zsag090 (PMID 42017829). Originally available online 2026-04-22 (epub-ahead-of-print) but only received final print/PubMed indexing on 2026-08-14 — likely why it was missed by earlier daily sweeps keyed to indexing date. Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard group. n=28 long COVID, 19 ME/CFS, 28 healthy controls; overnight polysomnography with sleep-microstructure analysis (spindle coupling, slow-oscillation metrics). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC core record and NCBI eutils esummary (pubdate history) matched by DOI/PMID.

papers.title: Skeletal muscle properties in long COVID and ME/CFS differ from those induced by bed rest
papers.authors: Charlton BT, Slaghekke A, Appelman B, Eggelbusch M, Huijts JY, Noort W, Hendrickse PW, Bloemers FW, Posthuma JJ, van Amstel P, Goulding RP, Degens H, Jaspers RT, van Vugt M, Wüst RCI
papers.summary: Researchers compared muscle biopsies and exercise tests from people with long COVID and ME/CFS against healthy volunteers who had done 60 days of strict bed rest (used to mimic pure physical deconditioning). The long-COVID and ME/CFS patients had fewer small blood vessels in their muscles and more 'fast' muscle fibres that tire quickly — a pattern that did not match what bed rest alone produces — and the ME/CFS patients also showed extra loss of their fatigue-resistant ('slow') muscle fibres.
papers.why: Pushes back against the idea that ME/CFS and long-COVID muscle problems are just from being sedentary, pointing instead to a real, disease-specific process in the muscle — directly relevant to Klaus Wirth's skeletal-muscle theory of post-exertional malaise (PEM, a crash after activity), even though he wasn't part of this study.
papers.notes: Nature Communications, published online Jul 28, 2026 (preprint precursor medRxiv 10.1101/2025.05.02.25326885). Amsterdam UMC/VU Amsterdam group (Wüst lab). Compared muscle biopsy + exercise-test findings in long-COVID and ME/CFS patients vs healthy controls who underwent 60 days of supervised bed rest; reduced capillary density and a shift toward glycolytic (fast, fatigable) fibre type in both patient groups not reproduced by bed rest alone, plus selective type-I (slow, fatigue-resistant) fibre atrophy specific to ME/CFS. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated but topically core to Wirth's skeletal-muscle/PEM pathomechanism hypothesis. Confirmed independently via Crossref DOI metadata (title/author list/journal match); Europe PMC does not yet have this DOI indexed (likely pending indexing lag), so Crossref + publisher-page redirect were used as the confirming sources per ROUTINE.md. Found via this run's fresh open-ended sweep, ~3 weeks after publication — flagging despite being slightly outside the normal 1-3 day recency window given it was not on the prior baseline and is high-relevance/high-profile (independently covered by Health Rising, 12 Aug 2026, and DutchNews).

papers.title: Data-driven subtypes of internalizing and functional somatic symptoms: A hybrid mixture modeling approach
papers.authors: Saini U, Wanders R, Oldehinkel AJ, Rosmalen JGM, van Loo HM
papers.summary: Using health-survey data from almost 73,000 adults in the Netherlands, researchers grouped people by their pattern of symptoms rather than by diagnosis label, looking at depression, anxiety, ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) together. One group, marked mainly by mental fog and fatigue, showed heavy overlap between ME/CFS-type symptoms and depression/anxiety symptoms, while pain-type symptoms formed their own separate group.
papers.why: Suggests some of the well-known overlap between ME/CFS and mood disorders may come from shared, non-specific symptoms (like fatigue and poor concentration) rather than the conditions truly being the same illness — relevant to the case for needing objective biomarkers to draw a clear line between them.
papers.notes: General Hospital Psychiatry, vol. 102, published online Aug 11, 2026. University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG) group. Cross-sectional mixture-modeling analysis of 72,919 adults in the Dutch Lifelines Cohort Study; six symptom-based classes identified (Healthy, Pain, Tension/Pain, Anxiety, Cognition/Fatigue, Depression), with ME/CFS, fibromyalgia and IBS criteria symptoms analyzed alongside major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. Borderline scope call — a broader functional-somatic/internalizing-symptom nosology study rather than an ME/CFS-dedicated paper, but ME/CFS is explicitly named and analyzed (confirmed via full Europe PMC abstract, which lists 'myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)' as one of the three functional disorders studied); included on the same precedent as the already-tracked mao-2026-depression-disease-history-mecfs entry (diagnostic-overlap/nosology papers). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (full abstract match) and Crossref DOI metadata (title/authors/journal match).

papers.title: Experimental hypoxia to probe neuro-metabolic and vascular dysregulation in ME/CFS: a multimodal proof-of-concept MRI study
papers.authors: Bader V, Estermann K, Niess E, Zrzavy T, Fischmeister F, Haider T, Ludwig B, Barkhof F, Mutsaerts H, Kasprian G, Niess F, Bogner W, Kollndorfer K, Haider L
papers.summary: 26 people with ME/CFS and 27 healthy people had brain scans (MRI) while breathing normal air and then air with less oxygen (a controlled, mild low-oxygen test). Patients' brains showed higher lactate (a byproduct of making energy without enough oxygen) even before oxygen was lowered, and their brain blood-flow response to low oxygen varied far more than in healthy people, alongside a slightly smaller brainstem.
papers.why: Gives direct brain-imaging evidence for the 'virtual hypoxia' idea in ME/CFS — that cells struggle to make energy properly and brain blood flow doesn't adjust normally under stress — and flags specific scan measures that could become an objective test for future trials.
papers.notes: Posted medRxiv 2026-08-10 (indexed 2026-08-12/13; PPR1297442). Medical University of Vienna group. n=26 ME/CFS vs 27 matched controls; single-session 3T multimodal MRI (volumetry, arterial spin labelling, MR spectroscopy) under normoxia + controlled hypoxia. This resolves the 2026-08-14 changelog's unconfirmed 'Bader et al.' forum lead — the previously-circulated DOI was wrong/garbled and resolved to an unrelated paper; this is the correct DOI, confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (full author list/abstract match). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated (though topically adjacent to Wirth's hypovolemia/vascular hypothesis).

papers.title: Cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure in relation to symptomatology and craniocervical anatomy in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Jolley C, Bragée B, Soinne L, Huhmar H, Billing H, Bertilson B, Sjögren P
papers.summary: In 34 ME/CFS patients who had a lumbar puncture (a needle test measuring fluid pressure around the brain and spine), just over a third had higher-than-normal pressure — and those patients were far more likely to feel better in the days right after the procedure, which temporarily lowers that pressure.
papers.why: Suggests a treatable fluid-pressure subgroup within ME/CFS, and that a simple pressure test could help identify who might benefit from pressure-lowering treatment.
papers.notes: Retrospective cross-sectional study, n=34. Swedish group (Bragée Clinic; Bertilson/Bragée are also behind the already-tracked bragee-2026-csf-proteomics entry). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via publisher DOI page (frontiersin.org).

papers.title: Persistent Neurological Symptoms After COVID-19 Lack Evidence of Adaptive CNS Immune Activation
papers.authors: Erhart DK, Balz LT, Giotaki I, Matits L, Gross R, Bachhuber F, Muench J, Kolassa I, Fitzner D, Uttner I, Lule D, Lewerenz J, Lange P, Tumani H
papers.summary: Spinal-fluid tests in 50 people with lingering post-COVID brain fog and fatigue, compared with 50 fully recovered people, found no extra brain immune activity or self-attacking antibodies in the affected group — even though their memory and fatigue were clearly worse.
papers.why: A notable negative finding arguing against ongoing brain inflammation or autoimmunity as the main driver of persistent post-COVID neurological symptoms, pointing research toward other explanations (such as the metabolic and vascular changes other new papers this run point to).
papers.notes: Ulm University group (senior author Tumani). n=50 vs 50, WHO post-COVID-condition criteria (substantially overlapping the ME/CFS population but not a strict PEM-gated diagnosis). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API.

papers.title: Orthostatic intolerance with small heart and/or disequilibrium in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: clinical update and paradigm shift
papers.authors: Miwa K
papers.summary: This review argues that dizziness and fatigue on standing in ME/CFS often comes from two under-recognized causes — an unusually small heart pumping less blood, and a subtle balance-system (inner-ear/brain) problem — not just blood pooling in the legs.
papers.why: Proposes specific, testable physical causes for a core disabling symptom, pointing toward different treatment targets (heart size/output, the balance system) than usual orthostatic-intolerance care.
papers.notes: Solo-author narrative review, no new patient data; echoes Wirth's own hypovolemia/small-heart hypothesis (already tracked as wirth-2026-hypovolemia-review) but is not Wirth-authored. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API.

papers.title: Biological Insights from Genome-Wide Association Studies and Whole Genome Sequencing of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Maccallini P
papers.summary: Combining genetic data from two large, separate ME/CFS studies (the UK's DecodeME and the US Million Veteran Program — almost 20,000 patients and 700,000 people without the illness combined), the strongest repeated signals pointed to brain genes, especially ones at 'glutamatergic synapses' (junctions between nerve cells that use the chemical messenger glutamate) — not genes active in blood.
papers.why: Independently combining two of the largest ME/CFS genetic datasets and finding the same brain-nerve-signal genes strengthens the case that ME/CFS involves a real, brain-based biological process, and flags specific pathways future drugs could target.
papers.notes: Found via the ~3-month backfill sweep (posted 2026-05-15, missed by prior daily runs). Meta-analysis of published GWAS summary statistics (19,470 cases / 699,111 controls) cross-checked against a whole-genome-sequencing rare-variant module. Distinct from a different, Zenodo-hosted Maccallini preprint already excluded in a prior run for venue reasons — this one is on Research Square, an already-accepted venue in this database (multiple existing entries use 10.21203 DOIs). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API.

papers.title: Association between myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and irritable bowel syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Rajabi N, Ramdass PVAK
papers.summary: Pooling 22 earlier studies, people with ME/CFS were found to be about seven times more likely to also have irritable bowel syndrome (IBS, a common gut condition) than people without ME/CFS — roughly 1 in 3 ME/CFS patients also has IBS.
papers.why: This strong, consistent overlap supports shared underlying biology (immune, nerve, and gut-signalling problems) and strengthens the case for gut-brain-axis-targeted research and care rather than treating fatigue and gut symptoms separately.
papers.notes: PROSPERO-registered systematic review + meta-analysis (22 studies reviewed, 18 pooled). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated; complements already-tracked gut-microbiome/tryptophan and genetic-overlap (ME/CFS-IBS) papers. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API.

papers.title: Perivascular spaces in neuropsychiatric post-COVID syndrome
papers.authors: Bernal J, Ilik SY, Mai H, Mattern H, Coello RD, Valdés-Hernández Md, Rocktäschel T, Reuken PA, Stallmach A, Wardlaw J, Opel N, Gaser C, Walter M, Ziegler G, Düzel E, Schreiber S, Besteher B
papers.summary: Brain scans of 116 people (59 with lasting post-COVID brain fog/fatigue, 57 without) looked at tiny fluid channels around brain blood vessels ('perivascular spaces', part of the brain's waste-clearance system). Older patients and those affected for longer had more enlarged channels, and this was linked to worse physical functioning.
papers.why: Adds a concrete, visible brain-imaging marker to the growing vascular/glymphatic (brain-fluid-drainage) evidence relevant to ME/CFS-type illness.
papers.notes: Jena group (senior authors Walter/Besteher — same group as the already-tracked bergmann-2026-metabolomic-neuropsychiatric-longcovid entry, likely overlapping cohort). n=116, exploratory cross-sectional. Cohort defined by 'neuropsychiatric post-COVID syndrome', not a strict ME/CFS/PEM diagnosis — included as a borderline call for the vascular-mechanism angle, same precedent as the already-tracked bergmann and mora-zetina entries. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API.

papers.title: Haptoglobin Phenotypes Stratify Post-Exertional Cognitive Dysfunction Associated with Altered Cerebral Oxygenation and Metabolic Signatures in Long COVID
papers.authors: Moezzi A, Elremaly W, Leveau C, Franco A, Nepotchatykh O, Armstrong CW, Moreau A
papers.summary: Haptoglobin is a blood protein that comes in different genetic variants (phenotypes). Researchers gave 44 long-COVID patients and 20 recovered people a 90-minute exertion challenge and found that people carrying one variant (Hp2-2) had a clear drop in thinking-test scores afterward, plus differences in brain oxygen levels and blood chemistry — while people with another variant (Hp1-1) stayed cognitively steady.
papers.why: Suggests a simple, already-testable genetic marker that could help explain why some post-viral patients get hit harder by post-exertional 'brain fog' than others, extending the same team's earlier ME/CFS finding to long COVID and pointing toward ways to predict who needs the most protection from overexertion.
papers.notes: IJMS 27(15):7000, published Aug 4, 2026. Université de Montréal / CHU Sainte-Justine / OMF ME/CFS Center group (Moreau lab); n=44 long-COVID vs 20 recovered controls; 90-minute exertion challenge with BrainCheck cognitive testing, cerebral oximetry, and metabolomics. Extends the group's earlier ME/CFS haptoglobin work to long COVID. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed independently via MDPI publisher page and DOI resolution.

papers.title: Identifying EEG biomarkers of fatigue and brain fog in long COVID: insights from rest and movement-related brain activity
papers.authors: Casado Sánchez M, Morales Fajardo K, Long S, Janaudis-Ferreira T, Duclos C, Boudrias MH
papers.summary: Using a cap of electrodes that measures brain electrical activity (EEG), researchers watched the brains of 20 long-COVID patients and 20 healthy people at rest and while doing a hand-grip task. The long-COVID patients showed a smaller brain-activity 'rebound' right after moving and a slower resting brain rhythm over the area that controls movement — patterns linked to fatigue and brain fog (trouble thinking clearly).
papers.why: Offers two concrete, measurable brain-wave signals as candidate objective tests for brain fog — a symptom that is otherwise hard to measure or prove to others — which could help diagnose it and track whether future treatments actually help.
papers.notes: J Clin Neurosci 153, indexed Aug 11, 2026 (McGill University group). n=20 long-COVID vs 20 healthy controls; resting-state + movement-related EEG (post-movement beta rebound, resting alpha frequency over sensorimotor cortex). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (title/authors/journal/DOI match); publisher page (ScienceDirect/Elsevier) blocked by login wall for direct verification.

papers.title: Impact of immunoadsorption on autoantibodies and physical performance in post-COVID patients: a prospective exploratory study of 18 participants
papers.authors: Wossidlo C, Steinbeck F, Geerdes-Fenge H, Sombetzki M, Mitzner S, Loebermann M, Reisinger EC, Koball S
papers.summary: Immunoadsorption is a treatment that filters antibodies out of the blood. In 18 post-COVID patients with raised levels of antibodies that mistakenly target the body's own stress-hormone receptors, the treatment clearly lowered those antibody levels — but the drop faded back within 3-6 months, and it did not improve how well patients performed on objective physical tests, only slightly easing self-reported pain and fatigue.
papers.why: A cautionary, negative-leaning result — from a different German university group, not Charité — on the same 'filter out the bad antibodies' approach behind Scheibenbogen's immunoadsorption trials, useful context for interpreting whether removing these antibodies alone is enough to relieve symptoms.
papers.notes: Infection, Aug 2026. University of Rostock group (Wossidlo/Steinbeck/Geerdes-Fenge/Sombetzki/Mitzner/Loebermann/Reisinger/Koball) — distinct from Charité's Scheibenbogen-led immunoadsorption programme (IMPACT/IA-Surv) already tracked in data/trials.json. n=18 post-COVID patients with elevated anti-GPCR autoantibodies; significant antibody reduction, reverting by 3-6 months; no significant objective physical-performance improvement, modest subjective pain/fatigue gains only. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated but topically adjacent (autoantibody/immunoadsorption hypothesis). Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (title/authors/journal/DOI match); Springer publisher page blocked by login redirect for direct verification.

papers.title: Long-term angiogenic and thromboinflammatory signatures in post-COVID-19 syndrome
papers.authors: Mora Zetina AA, Ortega Sanchez EF, Zuñiga Ascencio BS, Castorena Maldonado AR, Ahumada Topete VH, Torres Espíndola LM, Aquino Gálvez A, et al.
papers.summary: Researchers followed 32 people who had been hospitalized with COVID-19, three and a half years later. About two-thirds still had fatigue, breathlessness, or trouble concentrating, and their blood still showed high levels of proteins that drive blood-vessel growth (VEGF-D, angiopoietin-1) plus signs of a sluggish clotting system.
papers.why: Adds long-term evidence for a persistent blood-vessel and clotting abnormality behind lingering post-COVID fatigue — the same 'microclot'/vascular idea that also motivates some ME/CFS treatment approaches.
papers.notes: Published online Aug 7, 2026 (print vol. 29(4)). n=32 previously-hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 3.5-year follow-up; persistent symptoms (fatigue/dyspnea/concentration problems) in ~65%; elevated VEGF-D and angiopoietin-1, raised alpha-2-macroglobulin, prolonged prothrombin time. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via publisher DOI record (Springer, Angiogenesis journal).

papers.title: Multiomic and Spatial Profiling of Colorectal Tissue Reveals Viral Persistence and Immune Dysregulation in Long COVID
papers.authors: LaFranchi B, Maison DP, Vinden J, Rodriguez AE, Tout A, Grimbert L, et al., Peluso MJ, Henrich TJ
papers.summary: In gut-tissue samples and blood from 44 people with long COVID (compared to 13 who fully recovered), scientists found leftover pieces of the coronavirus still sitting in the gut lining. Nearby immune cells were both driving ongoing inflammation there and, oddly, failing to mount the response needed to fully clear the virus.
papers.why: Strengthens the 'viral persistence' theory — that leftover fragments of the original infection can keep the immune system in a low-grade fight — a leading explanation also considered for ME/CFS and a rationale for antiviral or immune-targeted treatment trials.
papers.notes: Posted bioRxiv Aug 7, 2026 (UCSF LIINC long-COVID cohort; senior authors Peluso MJ, Henrich TJ). n=44 long-COVID patients vs. 13 recovered controls; gut-biopsy + blood multiomics; SARS-CoV-2 antigen persistence with innate myeloid signalling driving chronic gut inflammation while suppressing viral-clearance pathways. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed — confirmed via bioRxiv DOI record.

papers.title: Peripheral metabolic signatures in patients with neuropsychiatric long COVID syndrome
papers.authors: Bergmann DL, Neugebauer S, Rocktäschel T, Dommaschk EM, Li M, Weuthen A, Refisch A, Blekic N, Kiehntopf M, Scherag A, Schiöth HB, Lim CK, Opel N, Walter M, Besteher B
papers.summary: Blood tests on long-COVID patients with mental and emotional symptoms — like brain fog and low mood — showed unusual levels of fats used for energy storage and transport (triglycerides and acylcarnitines). These changes tracked with how severe a person's fatigue and depression were, alongside differences seen on brain scans.
papers.why: Points to a disrupted fat/energy-processing system — the kind of mitochondrial 'energy crisis' already proposed for ME/CFS — as a possible shared driver of fatigue, and a plausible target for future metabolic treatments.
papers.notes: Posted medRxiv Aug 7, 2026 (Jena University group; senior authors Walter M, Besteher B). Serum metabolomics in long-COVID patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms vs. healthy controls; altered triacylglycerides/acylcarnitines correlated with fatigue/depression severity and cortical-thickness differences. Borderline scope call: focus is 'neuropsychiatric long COVID' rather than PEM-defined ME/CFS, included because fatigue severity is an explicit correlate and the metabolic/mitochondrial angle bears directly on ME/CFS mechanism hypotheses. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed — confirmed via medRxiv DOI record.

papers.title: Virus reactivation in acute and long COVID-19
papers.authors: Maguire C, Chen J, Rouphael N, and the IMPACC Network (180+ contributors, incl. Baden LR, Simon V, Davis MM, Nadeau KC, Krammer F)
papers.summary: In over a thousand people hospitalized with COVID-19, researchers found that dormant viruses many people already carry — like Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus (both common herpesviruses) — often 'wake up' and become active again during severe COVID-19, even in people whose immune systems were otherwise working normally. A group of usually-harmless viruses called anelloviruses also reactivated, and unlike the herpesviruses, this reactivation persisted for months afterward and was specifically linked to going on to develop long COVID.
papers.why: Adds large-scale evidence for a leading theory of what drives long COVID and ME/CFS-like illness: that reactivated 'sleeping' viruses keep the immune system on edge long after the original infection is gone, which is the same rationale behind antiviral and immune-modulating treatment approaches being tested in ME/CFS.
papers.notes: Nature, published online Aug 5, 2026. IMPACC (Immunophenotyping Assessment in a COVID-19 Cohort) Network study, n=1,154 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, longitudinal multi-omic profiling; herpesvirus (EBV, CMV) reactivation correlated with acute disease severity/inflammation; anellovirus reactivation persisted into convalescence and was specifically associated with long COVID. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: ADDRESS-LC: study protocol for a phase 2, triple-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of bezisterim (NE3107) in adults with long COVID
papers.authors: Markham P, Peluso MJ, Hsiang-Yi Chou S, McCorkell L, O'Quinn S, Reading C, Ahlem C, Petit CM, Yan J, Palumbo JM
papers.summary: This is a study plan (a protocol, not results yet) for a trial that will test bezisterim, a drug that calms a specific inflammation pathway in the body and brain, in 208 adults with long COVID who have had ongoing fatigue and 'brain fog' (trouble thinking clearly) for at least three months. Half will get the drug and half a placebo (dummy pill) for 12 weeks, with neither patients nor doctors knowing who got which.
papers.why: Tests the idea that ongoing brain inflammation — possibly from a lingering viral trace or an overactive immune response — drives long COVID's fatigue and brain fog, using a drug already tested for other brain-inflammation conditions; worth watching for when results are published, though this paper itself reports no outcomes yet.
papers.notes: BMJ Open 16(7), e-published Jul 24, 2026. Sponsor BioVie Inc.; phase 2 protocol only (n=208 planned), bezisterim (NE3107, an oral anti-inflammatory targeting the TLR/NF-κB pathway), 20mg twice daily vs placebo, 12 weeks, US-based trial (no German site — tracked on the papers side only, per ROUTINE.md papers are not Germany-restricted). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (title/authors/journal/volume/issue/DOI match).

papers.title: Central origin of fatigability in Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome revealed by multimodal neuroimaging
papers.authors: Bedard P, Knutson KM, McGurrin PM, Vial F, Popa T, Horovitz SG, Hallett M, Nath A, Walitt B
papers.summary: In a hand-grip strength test, people with ME/CFS and healthy people could squeeze just as hard at their very strongest, but the ME/CFS patients tired out much sooner. Brain and muscle activity recordings showed that as healthy people got tired, their brain and muscle signals ramped up to compensate — but in ME/CFS patients, this compensating brain signal barely increased at all.
papers.why: Suggests the fatigue in ME/CFS starts in how the brain drives and compensates for tired muscles, not in the muscles themselves — pointing researchers toward the brain and nervous system, not just the body, when looking for treatments for exhaustion and post-exertional crashes.
papers.notes: NeuroImage: Clinical, published online Jul 28, 2026. NIH Intramural group (Walitt/Nath/Hallett) — the same team behind the already-tracked walitt-2024-nih-deep-phenotyping study. n=15 ME/CFS vs 19 healthy controls; combined EEG/fMRI during a grip-force fatigue task. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Elsevier/ScienceDirect DOI record.

papers.title: The role of disease history score in the association between depression history and current myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Mao S, Wu L
papers.summary: Using health survey data from over ten thousand US adults, researchers found that people who had been depressed in the past were more likely to currently have ME/CFS. Much of this link could be explained by a broader pattern of past illnesses and health problems (a combined 'disease history score'), rather than depression itself directly causing ME/CFS — and the link was stronger in women and older adults.
papers.why: Helps untangle a long-running debate over whether depression and ME/CFS overlap because one causes the other, or because both simply reflect a person's overall burden of past illness — relevant to arguments that ME/CFS should be assessed in its full health context rather than reduced to a psychiatric diagnosis.
papers.notes: Frontiers in Public Health 14, published Jul 21, 2026. Cross-sectional mediation analysis of 2021-2023 US NHIS survey data; depression history associated with higher current-ME/CFS odds (OR 1.61), ~44-47% mediated by a composite disease-history/multimorbidity score, effect stronger in women and older adults. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers publisher page/DOI record.

papers.title: Feasibility and outcomes of crossflow membrane plasmapheresis for long COVID in Suriname: a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial
papers.authors: Bihariesingh-Sanchit R, Bansie R, Paltoe P, Ma R, Bustamente D, Ramesar D, Raghosing-Sanchit R, Codrington J, Ma-Bihariesingh I, Vreden S, van der Dijs F, Mangroo R, Simson M, Ramdhani N, Fung A Foek C, van 't Wout A, Diavatopoulos D, de Jonge M, Nierich A
papers.summary: In a small pilot study in Suriname, 18 people with long COVID were randomly given either real plasma-exchange treatment (filtering and replacing part of the blood's plasma, over 5 sessions) or a fake/sham version. People who got the real treatment reported meaningfully less fatigue three months later, while the sham group did not improve — but the study was too small to prove the real treatment was definitely better than the sham, and no serious side effects occurred.
papers.why: Adds early, though inconclusive, evidence that filtering blood plasma may ease long-COVID fatigue — a related idea to the immunoadsorption (antibody-filtering) trials Scheibenbogen's group runs in ME/CFS — with the authors themselves calling for a larger trial to confirm whether the effect is real.
papers.notes: Posted F1000Research Aug 5, 2026 — an open-access, post-publication-peer-review platform (not a traditional journal, not medRxiv/bioRxiv); included as a DOI-confirmed edge-case venue on the same footing as the Research Square preprints already tracked in this database (e.g. dehlia-2026-gene-expression-drug-repurposing, maes-2026-physio-affective-phenome-longcovid, wielscher-2026-decodeme-mendelian-randomization). Pilot RCT, n=18, crossflow membrane plasmapheresis (TPE) vs sham, 5 sessions, long COVID; significant within-group fatigue improvement in the TPE arm at day 90 not matched in the placebo arm, but between-group difference not statistically significant; no serious adverse events. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via F1000Research DOI, indexed in Europe PMC. Also screened and excluded this run (out of scope — care-delivery guidance, not pathomechanism/biomarker/drug-target/treatment-trial/genetics): Hermisson J et al., 'Guidance on Home-Based Care for People with Severe ME/CFS: A Transdisciplinary Expert Statement' (Wiener Medizinische Wochenschrift, Jul 29 2026, doi 10.1007/s10354-026-01182-3) — a care-guidance expert consensus statement, held to the same standard as the previously-excluded LCovB/general-practice-perspectives papers. Also excluded: Abken et al. 'CureME participatory model' (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, Jul 2026) — research-methodology/community-engagement paper, not biomedical mechanism or treatment-trial results.

papers.title: Pipeline-optimized machine learning for chronic fatigue syndrome diagnosis: A lightweight, interpretable model using blood biochemical and metabolomic data
papers.authors: Li J, Cao H, Zhu Z, Zhai X, Xing A, Zeng S, Luo G, Sha Y, Li P, Li K
papers.summary: Using blood test results from a huge UK health database (over 68,000 people, including about 1,100 with chronic fatigue syndrome), researchers built a computer model that predicts who has CFS from ordinary blood markers — like urea, blood sugar, and vitamin D — with very high accuracy in this dataset. A separate genetic method suggested six of these blood markers may actually help cause the illness, not just be a side effect of it.
papers.why: Suggests a cheap, already-available blood panel could one day help flag CFS early, and adds genetic evidence that everyday metabolic markers may play a causal role — though it needs testing in other patient groups, and the UK Biobank 'CFS' cases were identified from health records rather than confirmed with strict ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
papers.notes: Comput Biol Chem 123, epub 2026-03-03, print Aug 2026. PMID 41791269. UK Biobank cohort, 1,137 CFS cases vs 66,838 controls; tested 7 imputation x 9 feature-selection x 11 ML models; best model (Bayesian PCA imputation + random forest, 10 biomarkers + 3 covariates) reached accuracy 0.939, ROC-AUC 0.979. Mendelian randomization flagged 6 causally-linked biomarkers (urea, total protein, glucose, total bilirubin, leucine, vitamin D). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via PubMed (PMID 41791269) and Europe PMC REST record. Epub date (Mar 2026) sits right at the edge of the ~3-month recency window — likely missed by prior sweeps pending final volume/issue assignment and full indexing.

papers.title: The Mammillary Body-Fornix Gate in Long COVID: An exploratory structural and diffusion MRI study of tremor-like symptoms, internal vibrations, and neuromuscular fatigue
papers.authors: Ziaja CP, Young SY, Stark MS, Zurek G, Sedlacik J, Wright FM
papers.summary: Brain scans (structural and diffusion MRI, which maps the brain's internal wiring) compared 88 long-COVID patients who had unusual symptoms — tremors, internal 'vibration' feelings, and severe fatigue — against 34 healthy people. The patients showed differences in a small, deep brain structure pair called the mammillary bodies (involved in memory and relaying body signals) and in the nerve-fibre tracts connecting them, plus changes in the cerebellum (the brain's movement-coordination centre).
papers.why: Proposes a specific, physical brain-wiring explanation for the unusual tremor, internal-vibration and fatigue symptoms some long-COVID and ME/CFS patients report, giving researchers a concrete brain region to study further — but it's an early, small, not-yet-peer-reviewed exploratory study.
papers.notes: Posted medRxiv 2026-08-03. Structural + diffusion tensor MRI in 88 long COVID patients vs 34 healthy controls; three distinct mammillary-body volume patterns, narrowing at the superior tuberal-mammillary interface, reduced cerebellar peduncle volumes, altered diffusion metrics. Not yet peer-reviewed. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST record (DOI match).

papers.title: Associated factors and a risk prediction model for comorbid circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome: implications for early screening and sleep health management
papers.authors: Shao X, Yang F, Qin LL, Shi JN, Chen M, Ge WJ, Jiang TJ, Yue JW, Feng W, Wang JH, Zhang ZX
papers.summary: In a Chinese hospital study of 610 people with chronic fatigue syndrome, almost half also had a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder — a mismatch between the body's internal clock and normal sleep and wake times. The researchers built a simple scoring tool using factors like shift work, how severe the fatigue is, being female, and reduced deep sleep to help predict who has this sleep disorder.
papers.why: Offers doctors a quick screening tool to spot which CFS patients also have a treatable sleep-timing problem, so sleep health could be addressed alongside other CFS care — though it comes from a single Chinese hospital and it's unclear whether standard international ME/CFS diagnostic criteria were used.
papers.notes: Front Psychiatry, published 2026-07-20. PMID 42548707. Retrospective single-center study, 610 CFS patients (427 training/183 validation cohort); 48.7% had comorbid circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder; logistic-regression nomogram (shift work, fatigue severity, female sex, reduced slow-wave sleep) reached AUC 0.808 (train) / 0.767 (validation). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via PubMed record (PMID 42548707).

papers.title: Involvement of autoantibodies against G protein-coupled receptors in post-COVID condition and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Azcue N, Prada A, Del Pino R, Acera M, Fernández-Valle T, Ayo-Mentxakatorre N, Pérez-Concha T, Murueta-Goyena A, Lafuente JV, López de Munain A, Ruiz Irastorza G, Ribacoba L, Gabilondo I, Tijero-Merino B, Gómez-Esteban JC
papers.summary: Researchers measured autoantibodies — antibodies that mistakenly attack the body's own receptors for stress hormones and nerve signals — in the blood of 96 people with post-COVID condition, 59 with ME/CFS, and 36 healthy people. People with ME/CFS had higher levels of one such antibody (targeting a stress-hormone receptor called beta-2-adrenergic), and higher antibody levels went along with worse autonomic-nervous-system problems (like poor control of blood pressure and heart rate) and slower thinking speed.
papers.why: Adds another data point to the idea that misdirected antibodies attacking the body's own receptors help drive ME/CFS symptoms — the same idea behind Scheibenbogen's immunoadsorption trials (IMPACT, IA-Surv) that filter these antibodies out of the blood, though this is a different, Spanish (Basque Country) research group, not Wirth or Scheibenbogen themselves.
papers.notes: Sci Rep, published online May 5, 2026. PMID 42082542. Basque Country/Spain group (Biocruces Bizkaia / UPV-EHU, incl. López de Munain, Gabilondo). n=96 post-COVID, 59 ME/CFS, 36 healthy controls; anti-beta2-adrenergic-receptor autoantibody levels elevated in ME/CFS vs healthy, correlated with autonomic dysfunction and processing-speed measures. Distinct from the already-tracked azcue-2026-postcovid-mecfs-convergence entry (different journal/DOI/focus, overlapping but not identical author list). Backfilled this run — publication date (May 5) is close to the edge of the ~3-month recency window and was missed by prior daily sweeps; confirmed independently via Europe PMC REST API (title/authorString/journalTitle/pubYear/firstPublicationDate/PMID/DOI all match). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Also screened and excluded this run: Abanades et al. 'Micronutrition as a Therapeutic Strategy to Restore Mitochondrial Function in ME/CFS and Fibromyalgia' (Preprints.org, posted Jul 20, 2026, doi 10.20944/preprints202607.1446.v1) — a narrative review/future-trial-proposal with no new patient data, posted to Preprints.org, a lower-tier preprint venue only accepted in this database as an exception for Wirth-authored papers per ROUTINE.md; not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored, so held to the standard medRxiv/bioRxiv/peer-reviewed bar and not added.

papers.title: Circulating extracellular vesicles-microRNAs as potential biomarkers for the identification of ME/CFS: differentiating fatigue-related conditions
papers.authors: Eguchi A, Kuratsune H, Nakatomi Y, Yasui T, Nakagawa R, Watanabe Y, Fukuda S
papers.summary: Researchers compared tiny particles that cells release into the blood (extracellular vesicles) and the small RNA snippets they carry (microRNAs) in people with ME/CFS, people with ordinary chronic fatigue, and people with depression. ME/CFS patients had a distinct pattern of these particles and about 62 microRNAs that stood out compared to the other groups, pointing to disrupted nerve-cell and cell-structure pathways.
papers.why: Adds to a growing set of blood-based candidate markers that could eventually help doctors tell ME/CFS apart from look-alike conditions like depression or general tiredness, something there is currently no reliable test for — though this is a small, early exploratory study that needs replication in larger groups.
papers.notes: J Transl Med 24(1):979, published Jul 27, 2026. PMID 42533331. Osaka group (Eguchi/Kuratsune/Nakatomi/Watanabe/Fukuda), small exploratory cohort comparing ME/CFS vs. idiopathic chronic fatigue vs. depression by EV-microRNA profiling; ~62 differentially expressed microRNAs (incl. miR-21-5p, let-7f-5p, miR-26b-5p, miR-20a-5p) implicated in neuronal/cytoskeletal pathways. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed independently via PubMed record (PMID 42533331) and Springer/J Transl Med publisher page redirect from the DOI.

papers.title: Molecular hydrogen as a treatment for ME/CFS: a mini-review of clinical evidence and mechanistic rationale
papers.authors: Friedberg F, LeBaron TW
papers.summary: This mini-review looks at hydrogen-rich water — ordinary water with extra dissolved hydrogen gas — as a possible ME/CFS treatment. It calms harmful cell damage (antioxidant effect), reduces inflammation, and may help the cell's energy factories (mitochondria) work better. Three small early studies found it feasible and modestly helpful for fatigue, with mild side effects.
papers.why: A low-cost, low-risk supplement with early but weak evidence for reducing fatigue — worth watching, though the studies so far are small, not blinded, and rely on patients' own symptom reports rather than objective measurements.
papers.notes: Published Mar 18, 2026 (Frontiers in Medicine, vol. 13, Translational Medicine section) — newly found this run (missed by prior searches, similar to the earlier-missed wirth-2026-hypovolemia-review). Narrative mini-review of 3 small pilot studies (same research team) of hydrogen-rich water in ME/CFS; authors call for larger, blinded trials with objective biomarkers. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers journal article page. Also screened and excluded this run (fails papers scope — healthcare-delivery/care-pathway studies, not pathomechanism/biomarker/drug-target/treatment-trial/genetics): Aung/Scuffell et al., 'General Practice Perspectives on Post-Infection Conditions' (medRxiv, Jul 17 2026, UK GP scoping review + survey) and Burchardi/Scheibenbogen et al., 'LCovB' study protocol (PLoS One, Jul 9 2026, Charité post-COVID care-pathway mixed-methods study) — both are care-delivery protocols/surveys, not biomedical mechanism or treatment-trial-results papers. Also excluded: Ben Amar et al. 'epigenetic signatures in chronic pain' (Epigenomics, Jul 22 2026) — general chronic-pain topic, not ME/CFS-specific. Also excluded: Kuns et al. 'The State of Chronic Fatigue' PEM systematic review (Arch Phys Med Rehabil 107(5):e191, doi 10.1016/j.apmr.2026.02.468) — appears to be a conference-abstract-supplement entry (page 'e191'), not a full peer-reviewed article, so held to a lower-confidence bar than the mini-review above; not entered pending the full paper.

papers.title: Multimodal approach to identify neuropsychophysiological subgroups in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and their relevance for rehabilitation
papers.authors: Dooms Y, Qiu L, Coppieters I, Vergaelen E, Claes S, Dupont P, Hehl M, Cuypers K, Engler H, Dombrowski K, Verbeke K, Van den Bergh O, Raes J, Van Oudenhove L, Van Den Houte M, Bogaerts K
papers.summary: This is a study protocol (a research plan, not results yet) describing a planned Belgian study that will test 115 ME/CFS patients and 55 healthy people with a wide mix of measurements — inflammation markers, brain scans for inflammation, nervous-system function, gut bacteria, and stress-hormone responses — then follow patients through a rehabilitation programme to see which measurements predict who improves.
papers.why: Aims to sort ME/CFS patients into biological subgroups so future treatment (including rehabilitation) can be matched to what's actually driving each patient's illness, rather than one-size-fits-all — worth watching for when results are published.
papers.notes: Published online Jul 6, 2026 (eCollection Oct 2026). Study protocol only (n=115 ME/CFS, 55 controls planned), KU Leuven/Belgian group. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Elsevier/ScienceDirect publisher page.

papers.title: Agreement and reliability between the two-day 6-minute incremental step test and two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test in post COVID-19 condition for assessing post-exertional malaise: The REVEAL-study
papers.authors: Bomans S, Michotte N, El M'Rabet I, Jimenez Garcia B, Leemans L, Janssens P, Hanon S, De Waele E, Beckwée D
papers.summary: Researchers tested whether a simpler, cheaper 6-minute stepping test, done on two separate days, could replace the demanding two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET — a treadmill/bike test measuring oxygen use) for detecting post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity) in 25 people with post-COVID condition. The simpler step test only partly agreed with the CPET results, especially for oxygen-use and muscle-symptom measures, so it isn't yet reliable enough to fully substitute for the more demanding test.
papers.why: Finding an easier, less exhausting way to objectively measure PEM would make it much simpler to run future ME/CFS and post-COVID drug trials — this study is a needed reality-check showing the simpler option still needs refinement before it can be trusted.
papers.notes: Published Jul 14, 2026. Crossover design, n=25, one-month washout, Belgian group (UZ Brussel). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via PLOS ONE publisher page.

papers.title: Microstructural alterations in brain tissue of ME/CFS and long COVID using diffusion tensor imaging and diffusion kurtosis imaging
papers.authors: Singh TB, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Barnden L, Eaton-Fitch N, Huynh TH, Inderyas M, Thapaliya K
papers.summary: Using two advanced brain-scan techniques that map the tiny fibres connecting brain regions (diffusion tensor and diffusion kurtosis imaging), researchers compared brain structure in 37 people with ME/CFS, 19 with long COVID, and 27 healthy people. Both illnesses showed subtle differences from healthy brains, but in different areas and patterns — including changes in a motor-planning region and in the bundle of fibres linking the brain's two hemispheres — suggesting ME/CFS and long COVID are not simply the same condition at the brain-structure level.
papers.why: One of the first studies to directly compare brain wiring in ME/CFS versus long COVID rather than each against healthy people alone, adding evidence the two conditions may need to be studied and treated as biologically distinct rather than interchangeable.
papers.notes: Published Jul 17, 2026. Griffith University (Australia) neuroimaging group (Marshall-Gradisnik/Barnden/Thapaliya) — a recurring credible ME/CFS research team already in this database (thapaliya-2026-glymphatic-dti-alps, sasso-2026-trpm3-nkcell). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers journal article page.

papers.title: Handgrip strength in children, adolescents, and young adults with suspected myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
papers.authors: Mihatsch L, Schartner L, de Luna JL, Höhler C, Bucka L, Lovrenovic L, Eidenschink S, Schmuck B, Bienemann V, Christa C, Mittelstraß K, Hausruckinger A, Warlitz C, Michel K, Gerrer K, Freitag H, Scheibenbogen C, Pricoco R, Behrends U
papers.summary: Researchers measured hand-grip strength twice, an hour apart, in 147 young people (aged 10-25) being evaluated for ME/CFS and compared them with 83 healthy peers. The patients' grip strength and how it changed between the two tests differed from the healthy group, showing a real, measurable drop in muscle function — but the test alone could not reliably tell ME/CFS apart from other conditions that also cause tiredness.
papers.why: From Carmen Scheibenbogen's group: offers a simple, cheap, repeatable physical test that could serve as an objective way to track post-exertional muscle decline in children and teenagers for future drug trials, even though it can't yet stand alone as a diagnostic test.
papers.notes: Published online Jul 15, 2026. Pediatric/young-adult ME/CFS evaluation cohort (Charité/TU München group, incl. Behrends and Pricoco), 147 patients aged 10-25 vs 83 controls; two grip-strength sessions 60 minutes apart. Scheibenbogen is a co-author — HIGH PRIORITY. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/journal/date match).

papers.title: Association of rapamycin treatment with the modulation of purine metabolism, reduced microglial inflammatory responses, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism, and alleviation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS subjects: pilot findings from phase-II observational study
papers.authors: Gile B, Bulbule S, Toriola MA, Ruan BT, Marium S, Benko A, Grach S, Mueller M, Bateman L, Bell J, Yellman B, Berner J, Chheda B, Kaufman D, Gottschalk G, Roy A
papers.summary: In a small ongoing trial without a placebo group, ME/CFS patients took low-dose rapamycin (a drug that calms an overactive cell-growth signal) for three months. Blood and immune tests showed shifts in energy-related chemicals, calmer brain immune cells, better-working cellular batteries (mitochondria), and patients reported less fatigue.
papers.why: One of the few ME/CFS drug studies to show a treatment changing measurable body chemistry alongside symptom improvement, giving a testable biological reason — not just patient reports — to pursue rapamycin as a treatment lead.
papers.notes: PMID 42432754; registered as NCT06257420 (phase II observational pilot, Bateman Horne Center / Simmaron Research, USA). Published online Jul 10, 2026. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via journal DOI record.

papers.title: In Search of Lost Volume: The Potential Causes of Hypovolemia in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Klaus Wirth argues that people with ME/CFS often have too little fluid in their blood vessels (hypovolemia), caused by broken salt-and-water retention signals in the body, leaky small blood vessels, and starved muscle cells pulling fluid out of the blood during activity.
papers.why: From Wirth (Mitodicure): ties together low blood volume, dizziness on standing, and the post-exertional crash (a crash after activity) into one physical explanation, reinforcing the case for his group's muscle/circulation-focused treatment approach — but it's an early, not-yet-peer-reviewed hypothesis paper, so treat it as a working idea pending review.
papers.notes: Solo-author hypothesis/review paper posted Feb 2026 (v1) on Preprints.org — newly found this run (missed by prior searches). Included as an exception per ROUTINE.md's Wirth HIGH-priority provision, same lower-tier preprint-venue caveat as the already-tracked wirth-2026-connective-tissue-laxity. Not yet peer-reviewed.

papers.title: The efficacy of exercise in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Zhao L, Gou B, Zhang M
papers.summary: Combining results from 17 controlled trials with almost 2,000 ME/CFS patients, exercise programmes improved fatigue, sleep, and quality of life, but did not meaningfully improve heart/lung fitness or physical capacity.
papers.why: Exercise therapy is a historically controversial topic in ME/CFS because overexertion can trigger post-exertional malaise (a crash after activity). This large pooled analysis suggests exercise may ease some symptoms but is not a fix for the underlying physical limitation, supporting a cautious, symptom-management role rather than a cure.
papers.notes: Online Apr 15, 2026; print Aug 2026 (Vol 207). Meta-analysis of 17 RCTs, n=1,944. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Crossref/publisher record.

papers.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Wang S, Ren J, Fang S, Hao Q, Zhang YQ, Kong L, Fang M
papers.summary: Analysing 16 trials of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT, a talk therapy) for ME/CFS, guided self-help and one-on-one CBT reduced fatigue right after treatment. The specific ingredients that helped were goal-setting and acceptance-based techniques, while just teaching patients facts about the illness (psychoeducation) alone was possibly unhelpful.
papers.why: CBT is another historically contentious ME/CFS treatment. Rather than a blanket 'CBT works' or 'CBT doesn't work' claim, this pinpoints which specific ingredients may help versus backfire — useful for designing better-targeted psychological support alongside biomedical treatment.
papers.notes: Brain Behav 16(6), Jun 2026 (online May 31, 2026). Component network meta-analysis of 16 trials. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Crossref/publisher record.

papers.title: Efficacy of acupuncture-based traditional Chinese medicine therapies for chronic fatigue syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Li Y, Liang G, Xiao T, Xu L
papers.summary: Combining 8 trials with 715 patients, acupuncture reduced overall, physical, and mental fatigue more than control treatments, with no difference in side effects — though the authors themselves caution the trials were small and of uneven quality.
papers.why: Adds acupuncture to the list of non-drug approaches with some trial evidence for ME/CFS fatigue, though the low-confidence evidence base (small, uneven-quality trials, flagged by the authors themselves) means it should not be over-weighted against biomedical treatment approaches.
papers.notes: Front Neurol 17, Jun 24, 2026. Meta-analysis of 8 trials, n=715. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Crossref/publisher record.

papers.title: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) gene expression signatures for the identification of compounds targeting metabolism
papers.authors: Dehlia A, Alizada Z, Guthridge MA
papers.summary: Researchers combined two separate sets of ME/CFS patients' gene-activity data to find a shared pattern of 46 genes that behave differently in ME/CFS, then used a computer search to find existing drugs that might reverse that pattern. Three of the four candidate drugs — including pioglitazone, an already-approved diabetes medicine — gave a modest boost to energy production when tested on muscle cells grown in the lab.
papers.why: Flags specific already-approved drugs that target how cells produce energy, which could be tested in ME/CFS patients faster than developing a brand-new drug, and adds independent computational support to the energy-production theory of ME/CFS.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted Research Square Jul 5, 2026. Datasets GSE14577 and GSE227375; CMap L1000 drug-repurposing analysis; candidate compounds pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, tideglusib, MHY1485 tested on mouse myoblasts for mitochondrial membrane potential — all but rosiglitazone showed a modest significant increase. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC record.

papers.title: The physio-affective symptoms of Long COVID are strongly predicted by the severity of the acute infectious phase, and lowered antioxidants, nitric oxide, and alanine transaminase levels
papers.authors: Maes M, Tunvirachaisakul C, Semeão LdO, Michelin AP, Matsumoto AK, Brinholi FF, Barbosa DS, Zhang Y, Sodsai P, Hirankarn N, Almulla AF
papers.summary: Followed 71 long-COVID patients for six months and found that mood symptoms, CFS/ME-type fatigue symptoms, breathing problems, and nervous-system symptoms all rise and fall together as one combined package rather than being separate problems. How severe a person's original COVID infection was — including low levels of antioxidants and nitric oxide, molecules that help protect cells and blood vessels — strongly predicted how bad this combined symptom package became.
papers.why: Suggests it may be possible to predict, from measurements taken during the original COVID infection, which patients are heading toward the more severe, ME/CFS-like form of long COVID — useful for identifying who to watch closely or treat early.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted Research Square Jun 28, 2026 (indexed Jul 2). Same Maes-led international group as donchev-2026-gut-microbiome-mecfs-longcovid and petrov-2026-monocyte-dc-immunophenotyping already in this database. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC record.

papers.title: Risk factors for severe post-COVID condition in children, adolescents, and young adults
papers.authors: Donath Q, Haegele M, Schindler D, Welzhofer T, Christa C, Grabbe A, Leone A, Ilhan C, Weidmann C, Eberhartinger M, Bechtold S, Bursch N, Wolf H, Hieber H, Peo LC, Bucka LA, Stojanov S, Warlitz C, Alberer M, Gerrer K, Hausruckinger A, Mittelstrass K, Wendtner CM, Hoechstetter MA, Grübl A, Toepfner N, Pricoco R, Scheibenbogen C, Mihatsch LL, Behrends U
papers.summary: In a German study of 120 young people (7–25 years old) with long-lasting COVID symptoms, having 12 or more symptoms during the original infection, plus dizziness or fainting-type symptoms (a sign of the body struggling to regulate blood flow when standing up), strongly predicted who would go on to develop the most severe, disabling form of the illness — 24% of whom were ultimately diagnosed with ME/CFS.
papers.why: Gives doctors an early-warning checklist for spotting which children are at risk of the most severe, ME/CFS-associated outcome after COVID, potentially enabling earlier intervention. Scheibenbogen is a co-author — HIGH PRIORITY.
papers.notes: PMID 42082813. Eur J Pediatr 185(5):344. Published May 4, 2026. German multi-centre paediatric long-COVID cohort (n=120, ages 7-25). Scheibenbogen (Charité) co-author — HIGH PRIORITY. Confirmed via PubMed record (full author list, abstract, DOI).

papers.title: Disrupted glymphatic function and its relationship with sleep and cognitive impairment in ME/CFS assessed via DTI-ALPS
papers.authors: Thapaliya K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Inderyas M, Barnden L
papers.summary: Using a brain-scan technique that measures how well the brain clears waste while a person sleeps, researchers found that people with ME/CFS (31 patients vs 27 healthy people) have a noticeably weaker brain 'cleaning' system than healthy people, especially on the right side of the brain — and those with worse sleep and worse concentration/memory problems had the weakest waste-clearance.
papers.why: Points to a concrete physical mechanism — sluggish brain waste removal during sleep — that could help explain the brain fog and sleep disruption common in ME/CFS, and gives researchers a new measurable target for future biomarker or treatment studies.
papers.notes: Frontiers in Neuroscience, published Jun 19, 2026. Griffith University (Australia) neuroimaging group (Marshall-Gradisnik/Barnden), a recurring credible ME/CFS research team. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Frontiers journal article page (title/authors/date/DOI/abstract).

papers.title: Immunoadsorption Versus Sham Treatment for Post-COVID Syndrome: A Randomised Sham-Controlled Crossover Trial
papers.authors: Stortz M, Kommer A, Meineck M, Boedecker-Lips SC, Claßen P, Tomalla V, Rausch F, Lang LS, Wild PS, Schmidtmann I, Weinmann A, Kraus D, Weinmann-Menke J
papers.summary: In this German trial (Mainz), 40 people with long-term post-COVID symptoms and high levels of self-attacking antibodies had those antibodies filtered out of their blood (immunoadsorption), compared with a fake (sham) version of the same procedure. The real treatment did remove the antibodies as intended, but patients did not feel any better than those who got the sham treatment, and side effects were more common with the real treatment.
papers.why: This is a rigorous, placebo-controlled negative result for a treatment approach (removing 'self-attacking' antibodies) that other German trials — including Scheibenbogen's — are also testing in post-COVID/ME-CFS, so it's an important caution: filtering out these antibodies doesn't automatically translate into symptom relief, at least in this dosing/design.
papers.notes: Lancet Reg Health Eur, Vol 67 (Aug 2026 print; e-pub Jun 11, 2026). University Medical Center Mainz (IAMPOCO trial). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Elsevier publisher page and Europe PMC record.

papers.title: Insights into Pathophysiological Pathways in ME/CFS Through Genetic Correlation and Mendelian Randomization
papers.authors: Wielscher M, Vincenzi L, Weninger WP, Schernhammer ES
papers.summary: Using genetic data from the large DecodeME study (over 15,000 people with ME/CFS), researchers looked for genes shared between ME/CFS and other conditions, and tested whether some blood markers might actually cause ME/CFS risk rather than just being correlated with it. They found that having naturally more mitochondrial DNA (the energy-factory part of cells) seemed protective, while two markers of inflammation and blood-clotting activity seemed to raise risk.
papers.why: This is genetic evidence — not just an association in sick patients — pointing to cellular energy production and low-grade inflammation/clotting as likely causes rather than side effects of ME/CFS, which supports the biological rationale behind drugs targeting mitochondria or clotting/inflammation.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. v1 posted Apr 10, 2026; v2 Apr 21, 2026. Medical University of Vienna group. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Direct Research Square fetch blocked (403); confirmed via Europe PMC record (title/authors/DOI/date/key finding) plus preprint-report secondary summary.

papers.title: Global and local genetic overlap among ME/CFS, irritable bowel syndrome and psychiatric traits: a hypothesis-generating analysis
papers.authors: Lee JH
papers.summary: This genetic study compared ME/CFS with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), depression, and loneliness using large genetic databases.
