papers.title: Wearable Heart Rate Variability Monitoring, Autonomic Dysfunction and Post-exertional Malaise in Long COVID: An Observational Study
papers.authors: Ruijgt TM, Slaghekke A, Ellens A, Janssen KW, Wüst RCI
papers.summary: Using wearable heart-rate monitors over several days on 121 people with long COVID and 21 healthy people, researchers found that patients' heart-rate variability (a measure of how well the body's automatic 'rest and recover' nervous system is working) was lower around exercise and during sleep. This recovery signal stayed abnormal for a full 24 hours after exertion, especially once activity crossed a specific intensity level.
papers.why: Gives a concrete, wearable-measurable warning line for how much exertion triggers a crash (post-exertional malaise), which could help patients pace themselves and give future drug trials an objective way to measure improvement.
papers.notes: Published online Jul 25, 2026 (Sports Medicine, ahead of print). Dutch group (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam), n=121 long-COVID vs 21 healthy controls, multi-day wearable HRV monitoring around exercise and overnight. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/journal/date match).

papers.title: High Quality Analysis of Circulating Biomarkers Reveals No Evidence of Elevated Inflammatory Markers in a Long COVID Cohort Recruited at a Primary Care Center
papers.authors: Torres ML, Lerma-Irureta D, Ibañez-Ruiz J, Lucas A, Magallón-Botaya R, Schoorlemmer J
papers.summary: Using a more precise blood test than earlier studies, researchers re-measured common inflammation markers (CRP, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6) in long-COVID patients recruited from a Spanish primary-care clinic, and found no evidence these markers were raised compared with recovered or healthy people.
papers.why: A negative finding that argues against simple blood-inflammation markers as a reliable way to diagnose or explain long COVID, pushing the search for a cause toward other biology (such as microclots or immune-cell dysfunction) instead.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted medRxiv Jul 28, 2026 (indexed Jul 30). Spanish group (Zaragoza primary care). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/date match).

papers.title: An Open-Label Feasibility Study of Remdesivir in Long COVID: Results from the ERASE LC Trial
papers.authors: Faghy MA, Chynoweth J, Barnett A, Skipper L, Allgar V, Neilens H, Sands K, Lord A, Hambly H, Aspinall P, Rollinson C, Strain W, Owen R, Thomas C, Grigg M, Kranen S, Mokbel K, Razak H, Ashton R, Maidment I, Bewick T
papers.summary: 73 people with long COVID in the UK received a 5-day course of the antiviral drug remdesivir (given through an IV drip) to test whether this was feasible and safe — not yet a full test of whether it works. Almost everyone completed treatment safely, and patients reported some improvement in fatigue and walking ability, but the authors say a proper randomised trial with a comparison group is still needed to know if the drug itself caused the improvement.
papers.why: The first test of an antiviral drug (rather than an immune-calming one) for long COVID, suggesting a lingering virus may still be worth targeting even long after the original infection — a live question in ME/CFS-type illness as well.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted medRxiv ~Jul 26-28, 2026. UK group, Gilead Sciences-funded (Gilead manufactures remdesivir). Open-label feasibility trial (n=73), no control arm — not yet an efficacy result. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/date match).

papers.title: Exploratory Dried Blood Spot Metabolomics Identifies Pathway-Level Convergence with ME/CFS Biology in a Self-Reported PEM-like Fatigue Phenotype
papers.authors: Hauguel P, Anctil N, Noel L
papers.summary: Finger-prick blood-spot samples from 1,784 people in a large community health study were tested for metabolic chemicals. People who reported a post-exertional-malaise-like 'crash after activity' pattern showed the same kinds of energy-production, fat, and stress-hormone chemical differences previously found in diagnosed ME/CFS patients — using a much larger, cheaper sample method than earlier studies.
papers.why: Suggests ME/CFS-type metabolic disturbance may be detectable even from self-reported crash-after-exertion symptoms in the general population, using an inexpensive finger-prick test — a possible low-cost screening or biomarker approach at a much larger scale than prior blood studies.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted medRxiv Jun 10, 2026 (missed by prior runs, found via a 3-month sweep this run). n=1,784 community cohort, dried-blood-spot metabolomics, self-reported PEM-like phenotype (not a clinical ME/CFS diagnosis). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/date match).

papers.title: Rationale and Design of RECOVER-ENERGIZE: A Platform Clinical Trial of Interventions for Exercise Intolerance With and Without Post-exertional Malaise in Long COVID
papers.authors: Friedly J, Bateman L, Berdan LG, Casaburi R, Erdmann N, Felker GM, Itchon-Ramos N, Keteyian SJ, MacIntyre N, O'Brien L, Reist C, Rossiter HB, Silverstein A, Taylor E, Pike Welch H, Yanez ND, Zimmerman KO, Make B
papers.summary: This is a trial-design paper, not results yet: it lays out a large US 'platform trial' — a flexible design that can test several treatments over time within one shared structure — for exercise intolerance and post-exertional malaise in long COVID, run through the NIH's RECOVER initiative.
papers.why: A major, NIH-funded piece of trial infrastructure signalling a coming wave of rigorously tested treatments specifically for post-exertional malaise and exercise intolerance, an area with very few good trials so far; includes well-known ME/CFS exercise-physiology researchers (Lucinda Bateman, Harry Rossiter). Worth tracking for when the first results post.
papers.notes: Preprint, not yet peer-reviewed, posted medRxiv Jun 3, 2026 (missed by prior runs, found via a 3-month sweep this run). Trial-design/protocol paper for a platform RCT under NIH's RECOVER initiative; no efficacy results yet. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API (title/authors/date match).

papers.title: ME/CFS and the thalamus as a precision gate: what reversible thalamocortical connectivity reveals about central gain in post-infectious fatigue
papers.authors: Strube A
papers.summary: This is a commentary (an expert opinion piece, not a new experiment) that builds on a recent Charité study showing that a deep brain relay station called the thalamus—which filters and passes along sensory and body signals—works differently in ME/CFS patients, and partly shifted toward a healthy pattern after hyperbaric oxygen therapy (breathing pure oxygen in a pressurized chamber). The author proposes that many ME/CFS symptoms that seem unrelated—oversensitivity to light/sound/touch, pain, dizziness on standing, and brain fog—could all be explained by this same brain 'gatekeeper' being turned up too high, rather than being separate problems.
papers.why: Offers a single, unifying brain-based explanation for ME/CFS's very varied symptoms, which could help researchers design treatments that target this one control point instead of treating each symptom separately—though it's an opinion piece built on one earlier study, not new patient data, so the idea still needs direct testing.
papers.notes: J Transl Med, published online Jul 29, 2026. Solo-author commentary/hypothesis piece building directly on the already-tracked kim-2026-hbot-mecfs study (Charité/Scheibenbogen HBOT + thalamic resting-state connectivity cohort, J Transl Med Jun 5 2026): proposes a predictive-processing/'central gain' framework in which altered thalamocortical gating unifies sensory hypersensitivity, pain, orthostatic intolerance, and cognitive fog in ME/CFS, and flags that causality (vs. correlation with a vascular/oxygen intervention) still needs testing across exertion/PEM. Not itself Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored but directly engages their group's data. Confirmed via Crossref API record (title/author/journal/date/DOI all match); not yet indexed in Europe PMC as of this check (recent-publication indexing lag).

papers.title: Altered TRPM3-Dependent Cytosolic and Mitochondrial Calcium Influx in Natural Killer Cells of Post-COVID-19 Condition Patients
papers.authors: Magawa CT, Eaton-Fitch N, Muraki K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, et al.
papers.summary: Researchers looked at natural killer (NK) cells — a type of immune cell — in 8 people with long-lasting post-COVID illness and 8 healthy people. The patients' NK cells had a faulty calcium "gate" (a channel called TRPM3): too little calcium got into the main body of the cell, but too much built up inside the cell's energy-making parts (mitochondria), and the cells barely responded when stimulated.
papers.why: The same faulty TRPM3 calcium channel was first found in ME/CFS immune cells, so finding it again in post-COVID illness supports the idea that ME/CFS and post-COVID share a common underlying immune and energy problem — a possible shared target for future treatments.
papers.notes: Griffith University NCNED group (Australia), not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored. Small study (n=8 vs 8). Confirmed via journal DOI record.

papers.title: Investigation of BOLD signal intensities in long COVID patients using 7T functional MRI
papers.authors: Inderyas M, Thapaliya K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, Barnden L
papers.summary: Using an extra-powerful (7 Tesla) brain scanner, researchers compared brain activity in 19 people with long COVID and 27 healthy people while they did a thinking task. The long-COVID patients had weaker brain-activity signals in the regions that handle attention and error-checking, and this was linked to slower thinking and more pain.
papers.why: Gives high-resolution evidence that long-COVID brain fog and fatigue come with real, measurable changes in brain activity, rather than just being tiredness — from a group that also studies ME/CFS brain imaging, strengthening the case for a shared biological basis.
papers.notes: NCNED group (Griffith University, Australia), not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored. Confirmed via journal DOI record.

papers.title: Brain dynamics of attentional, default-mode and limbic networks are disrupted at rest in post-COVID-19 syndrome
papers.authors: Cahart MS, O'Daly O, Cai Z, Mariani N, Borsini A, Mondelli V, Eiff B, Rota S, Nicholson T, Rida L, Hampshire A, Dipasquale O, Fernandes L, Turkheimer F, Williams SCR, Martins D
papers.summary: Resting-state brain scans of 20 people with post-COVID syndrome and 20 healthy people found that patients' brains spent less time in an "alert, paying-attention" pattern and more time in an "inward-focused, emotional" pattern.
papers.why: Suggests post-COVID fatigue and brain fog may involve the brain getting "stuck" in a less outward-focused mode — a possible objective brain signature that could one day help diagnose the condition or judge whether a treatment is working.
papers.notes: King's College London group, not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored. Confirmed via journal DOI record.

papers.title: A cardiometabolic perspective on post-exertional malaise in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and Long COVID
papers.authors: Westermeier F, Pretorius E, Untersmayr E, Bertinat R, Sepúlveda N, Fisman E
papers.summary: This opinion article argues that post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity that is the hallmark of ME/CFS) isn't just one system flaring up, but a breakdown in how the heart, blood vessels and metabolism coordinate with each other in the hours and days after exertion — especially in patients who also have obesity or type 2 diabetes.
papers.why: Proposes a broader way of studying and eventually treating PEM by tracking the heart and metabolism together over time after exertion, rather than looking at one body system at a time — a framework that could help design better drug trials aimed specifically at PEM.
papers.notes: Cardiovascular Diabetology 25:250, published online 2026-08-20 (PMID 42625219). Perspective/editorial, no new patient data. Co-authored by Etheresia Pretorius (prominent microclot/coagulation researcher) — topically adjacent to the vascular/microcirculation pathomechanism space Wirth also works in, but not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored. Confirmed via PubMed/Europe PMC and publisher DOI record.

papers.title: Microvascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction across the post-COVID-19 spectrum: a prospective observational case-control study
papers.authors: Wallraven T, Günthner R, Lethen I, Ribeiro A, Lech M, Oertel FC, Reeß LG, Haller B, Streese L, Hanssen H, Basta-Wunderle M, Schmaderer C
papers.summary: Using a special camera that watches how the tiny blood vessels at the back of the eye react to a flickering light, researchers compared 96 healthy people, 102 people who recovered fully from COVID-19, and 102 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms (62 of whom met full ME/CFS criteria). The vessels of post-COVID patients widened less in response to the flicker and were narrower at rest, and this problem was worst in the ME/CFS group, whose blood also showed higher levels of markers linked to inflamed, damaged blood-vessel walls.
papers.why: Offers a simple, non-invasive eye test as a way to spot and measure the blood-vessel problems thought to underlie ME/CFS, which could help diagnose patients earlier and track whether future vascular-targeted treatments are actually working.
papers.notes: BMC Medicine 24:456, published online 2026-08-19 (PMID 42625188), NCT05635552 ('All Eyes on PCS'). TU Munich (Dept. of Nephrology, lead) with Charité co-authors (Oertel, Reeß — Experimental & Clinical Research Center) but not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-authored. n=96 never-infected controls, 102 SARS-CoV-2-recovered, 102 post-COVID syndrome (62 meeting ME/CFS criteria); retinal vessel analysis (dynamic + static) showed reduced flicker-induced venular dilation, narrower retinal arterioles, and lower arteriolar-to-venular ratio in PCS patients (most pronounced in the ME/CFS subgroup, AUC=0.79), correlating with symptom burden and elevated IL-6/ICAM-1/VCAM-1. Confirmed via PubMed/Europe PMC and publisher DOI record.

papers.title: Persistent Hypercoagulability and Further Characterization of Microclot Complexes in Long COVID
papers.authors: Nunes M, Pereira Guerreiro CM, Pretorius JH, Venter C, Thierry AR, Fielding BC, Kell DB, Pretorius E
papers.summary: Blood was tested from 20 people with long COVID and 19 healthy people. The long-COVID patients' blood clotted faster and firmer than normal (called hypercoagulability), and contained more 'microclots' — tiny clumps of a misfolded blood protein that special dyes can detect sticking to them.
papers.why: Adds more detailed evidence for the microclot theory of long COVID and ME/CFS — the idea that abnormal, hard-to-dissolve clots clog small blood vessels and starve tissues of oxygen, from Etheresia Pretorius's group, the lab most associated with this research direction.
papers.notes: Posted medRxiv 2026-08-23. n=20 long COVID vs 19 healthy controls; viscoelastometry (clot strength/speed) plus fluorescence microscopy microclot quantification. Long-COVID-only cohort (no ME/CFS-diagnosed patients specifically), included per papers-track precedent of tracking long-COVID mechanism work relevant to ME/CFS (microclot theory). Co-author Pretorius also on the already-tracked westermeier-2026-cardiometabolic-pem-perspective entry. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/DOI match).

papers.title: Persistent Mitochondrial and Endothelial Dysfunction in Non-Hospitalized Patients with Long COVID
papers.authors: Ono R, Takayama S, Abe M, Arita R, Onodera K, Ishizawa K, Kanno T, Saito N, Kikuchi A, Abe T, Ishii T
papers.summary: 32 long-COVID patients in Japan were followed for 6 months. Two blood markers — one showing stress in the cell's 'power plants' (mitochondria) and one showing damage to the lining of blood vessels — stayed high in patients who hadn't gotten better, but dropped in those who improved. 91% of participants had fatigue as a main symptom.
papers.why: The authors directly link these findings to ME/CFS, arguing the same mitochondrial and blood-vessel problems seen here likely underlie ME/CFS fatigue too, and offer a simple blood test for tracking who stays stuck in prolonged illness.
papers.notes: Published online 2026-08-20. Tohoku University group. n=32 non-hospitalized long-COVID patients, 6-month longitudinal follow-up; serum GDF-15 (mitochondrial stress marker) and VCAM-1 (endothelial dysfunction marker) tracked against symptom trajectory. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed directly via Frontiers publisher page (title/authors/journal/date match).

papers.title: Circulating MicroRNA ratios as diagnostic biomarkers for long COVID with an independent validation cohort
papers.authors: Han E, Lukovic D, Müller-Zlabinger K, Hasimbegovic E, Schefberger K, Kastner N, Spannbauer A, Riesenhuber M, Nitsche C, Zelniker TA, Gyöngyösi M, Hamzaraj K
papers.summary: Medical University of Vienna researchers tested blood from 206 long-COVID patients and 71 healthy people, looking at ratios of tiny genetic messenger molecules (microRNAs) linked to mitochondrial and blood-vessel health. Two of these ratios were reliably lower in long-COVID patients in two separate patient groups, though the test's accuracy dropped when checked against an outside dataset.
papers.why: A step toward an objective blood test for long COVID that could plausibly extend to ME/CFS diagnosis, though the authors are upfront that it isn't accurate enough yet for clinical use.
papers.notes: Communications Medicine (Nature portfolio), published online 2026-08-20. Medical University of Vienna group. n=206 long-COVID patients vs 71 healthy controls, discovery + independent validation cohort; two mitochondrial/vascular-linked microRNA ratios found reduced but with reduced external validation accuracy. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated; not yet indexed in Europe PMC (very recent) — confirmed via Crossref DOI metadata (title/authors/journal/date match).

papers.title: EBV Reprograms B Cells in an Autoimmune-Like Fashion in Patients with COVID-19
papers.authors: Chen DG, Yuan D, Su Y, Magis A, Chu H, Goldman JD, Heath JR
papers.summary: In COVID-19 patients, the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, a common 'sleeper' virus most people already carry) can reawaken and reprogram the immune cells it infects (B cells) to act as if they're attacking the body's own tissue. People with more of these reprogrammed cells had worse lingering symptoms 2-3 months later.
papers.why: EBV reactivation is a long-standing suspect in both long COVID and ME/CFS; this gives a specific cellular mechanism — autoimmune-like B-cell reprogramming — for how a reawakened 'sleeper' virus could drive lasting illness.
papers.notes: Posted bioRxiv 2026-08-18 (PPR). Institute for Systems Biology, Seattle (prominent immune-monitoring/systems-immunology lab). Not yet peer-reviewed. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/DOI match).

papers.title: Orthostatic Dysfunction and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Close Reciprocal Relationship Beyond Cardiac Preload Failure and Hypoperfusion
papers.authors: Wirth KJ
papers.summary: Standing up puts extra strain on the body, and people with ME/CFS often feel worse when upright (orthostatic intolerance). This paper argues that standing doesn't just strain the heart and blood vessels — it may also directly overload muscle cells with calcium, the same overload process Klaus Wirth has proposed causes post-exertional malaise (PEM, a crash after activity).
papers.why: Proposes that simply standing — not only physical exertion — could trigger PEM-like crashes in severely ill ME/CFS patients through one shared cellular mechanism, tying together two of the illness's most disabling symptoms; it's Wirth's own hypothesis, so high priority to watch for follow-up evidence.
papers.notes: Posted Preprints.org 2026-08-25 (v1). Solo-authored hypothesis paper by Klaus Wirth (Mitodicure) — HIGH PRIORITY, Wirth-authored, same lower-tier preprint-venue caveat as other already-tracked Preprints.org Wirth entries (wirth-2026-hypovolemia-review, wirth-2026-connective-tissue-laxity). Direct fetch of preprints.org manuscript page returned HTTP 403; confirmed instead via doi.org redirect resolving to the correct preprints.org manuscript URL plus independent corroboration from a Science for ME forum thread quoting the abstract verbatim (title/author/DOI/mechanism match). Not yet peer-reviewed. Extends Wirth's Na+/K+-ATPase / NCX calcium-overload skeletal-muscle hypothesis (already tracked via wirth-2026-myasthenia-electrophysiology and the earlier skeletal-muscle reviews) to argue orthostatic stress alone, via impaired beta2-adrenergic Na+/K+-ATPase activity, can trigger the same PEM-causing calcium overload without physical exertion.

papers.title: VSL#3® supplementation improves fatigue in long COVID: results from the DELong#3 randomized placebo-controlled trial
papers.authors: Amoroso C, Marinoni B, Maragno P, Rimondi A, Bottaro F, Ciafardini C, Muià M, Honcharyuk I, Noviello D, Caridi B, Sommella EM, Bandera A, Gori A, Mantero M, Blasi F, Ferrucci R, Priori A, Strati F, Vecchi M, Facciotti F, Caprioli F
papers.summary: In this Italian trial ('DELong#3'), 48 adults with lasting fatigue after COVID-19 took either a high-dose multi-strain probiotic (a supplement of live gut bacteria, brand VSL#3®) or a placebo (dummy pill) for four weeks. People on the probiotic reported a much bigger drop in their fatigue than those on placebo, and the improvement was still there a month after they stopped taking it.
papers.why: It's one of the few placebo-controlled trials to show a measurable fatigue benefit in long COVID, and points to the gut microbiome (the community of bacteria living in the intestines) as a plausible, low-risk treatment target — though the trial is small and needs to be repeated in more people.
papers.notes: Br J Biomed Sci 83:16993, published online Jul 27, 2026 (PMID 42577968), indexed by Europe PMC 2026-08-13. University of Milan / Fondazione IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico group (Vecchi/Caprioli gastroenterology lab). RCT, n=48 (24/24) adults with post-COVID fatigue; 4 weeks high-dose VSL#3 vs placebo, with 4-week follow-up off treatment. Surfaced via The Sick Times' Aug 25 2026 research roundup (lead only) but independently confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/DOI match) before being recorded. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Registered as an NCT trial per Europe PMC's accession-number tagging (tmAccessionTypeList: nct) — not independently looked up this run.

papers.title: Early HHV-6 IgG and IgA responses during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection in relation to long COVID: a multicohort observational study
papers.authors: Choudhury A, Burry MJ Jr, Kwon WJ, Yin X, Rallistan A, Presti S, Ndakwah GS, Cheng EQ, Kalaycioglu M, Harris M, Frankovich J, Karlson EW, Bollyky J, Utz PJ, Prestwood TR
papers.summary: Researchers measured antibodies against a very common dormant virus most people already carry (HHV-6, a herpesvirus) in blood drawn right when people first caught COVID-19. One antibody pattern (high 'IgA' antibody against HHV-6) at that early point was linked to a higher chance of later developing long COVID, while a different pattern ('IgG' antibody) was linked to a lower chance.
papers.why: Adds evidence that a dormant, usually-harmless virus 'waking up' around the time of the original infection may help set someone up for long COVID/ME-CFS-like illness, and hints at an early blood test that might one day flag who is at risk before symptoms even start.
papers.notes: EBioMedicine 131:106455, published online Aug 27, 2026 (PMID 42660019), indexed by Europe PMC 2026-08-30. Stanford (Utz lab) with RECOVER-cohort collaborators; multicohort observational study of HHV-6 antibody responses during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection as a predictor of subsequent long COVID. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. A May 2026 SSRN preprint of the same work also exists; this peer-reviewed EBioMedicine version is the citable record. Confirmed independently via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/DOI match).

papers.title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for the treatment of long COVID (RECOVER-VITAL): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial
papers.authors: Baden LR, Shah NS, Liu STH, Cohen J, Moy J, Kumar A, McComsey GA, Chen P, Floris-Moore M, Singer NG, Fernandez I, Slandzicki AJ, Wiley Z, Kadl A, Kaminsky DA, Hsu H, Walker TA, Hope AA, Ostrosky-Zeichner L, Goldman JD, Peluso MJ, Patterson TF, Parthasarathy S, Mullington JM, et al., for the RECOVER-VITAL Clinical Trial Group
papers.summary: In this large US trial, 959 adults with long COVID (symptoms lasting 12+ weeks after COVID-19) were randomly given the antiviral drug Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) or a dummy pill for 15 or 25 days, to test whether hidden leftover virus is driving their symptoms. Whether people mainly had brain fog, dizziness/fast heart rate, or exercise intolerance (a crash after activity), the drug did not work better than placebo on any measure.
papers.why: This is the largest, most rigorous test yet of the idea that long COVID is caused by virus lingering in the body, and it found no benefit — a disappointing but important result that pushes research toward other explanations and treatments, including for the exercise-intolerance/PEM-type long COVID that overlaps with ME/CFS.
papers.notes: NCT05595369, NIH RECOVER Consortium. n=959 mITT across 3 pre-specified symptom phenotypes (cognitive n=332, autonomic n=334, exercise/PEM n=332), 69 US sites, enrolled Jul 2023-Sep 2024. Primary endpoint = day-90 change on phenotype-specific PROs (incl. a modified DePaul PEM short form for the exercise arm). No statistically significant benefit on any primary or secondary endpoint for either 15-day or 25-day regimen vs placebo; no safety signal (52 SAEs in 42/963, no deaths). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated but directly relevant to the German post-COVID/NAPKON trial landscape tracked on the trials side — a large negative RCT against the viral-persistence hypothesis. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/DOI/abstract match), corroborated by EurekAlert press release and a Science for ME forum thread quoting the paper.

papers.title: Fragile mitophagy and post-exertional malaise in long COVID: a hypothesis
papers.authors: Groysman R
papers.summary: This paper proposes a new explanation for why people crash one to three days after activity in long COVID (post-exertional malaise, PEM): damaged mitochondria (the cell's energy factories) get flagged for clean-up, but the clean-up process doesn't finish properly, so leftover mitochondrial debris keeps triggering inflammation long after the activity itself is over.
papers.why: A plausible new piece for the PEM puzzle — mitochondrial 'clean-up failure' rather than simply low energy — that could in principle be tested with existing lab methods, though it is one author's hypothesis with no new experimental data behind it yet.
papers.notes: Frontiers in Medicine (Hypothesis and Theory article), published online 2026-08-12. Solo author (Groysman R, 'Covid Institute', Plano TX — independent researcher, non-academic affiliation); lower-confidence tier similar to other tracked independent-researcher hypothesis pieces, but peer-reviewed at a legitimate (if high-volume) Frontiers journal. Hypothesis-only, no primary data. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated; conceptually complements already-tracked PEM mechanism entries (Wirth's Na+/K+-ATPase/calcium-overload hypotheses, the eNOS/two-threshold model, and the vascular/cardiometabolic perspective pieces). Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record and the Frontiers publisher page (full text fetched).

papers.title: A comparative analysis of computational clustering methods for symptom-based classification of long COVID
papers.authors: Green TD, McWilliams C, de Figueiredo L, Soares L, Pollack B, Cohen AK, Zhi-Xuan T, Falor T, Davis HE
papers.summary: Patient-researchers analysed survey answers from over 6,000 people with long COVID about 162 symptoms, using three different computer clustering methods to sort patients into subtypes. The three methods largely disagreed with each other about what the 'real' subtypes were, suggesting long COVID's symptom pattern is more of a continuous spectrum than a set of clear-cut categories — though people with more overall symptoms consistently also had worse post-exertional malaise (the crash after activity) and were more often women.
papers.why: A caution flag for the whole field of long-COVID/ME-CFS 'subtyping' research: which subtype a patient gets assigned may depend more on which statistical method a study happens to use than on a real biological grouping — which matters for how future trials pick and interpret patient subgroups.
papers.notes: Oxford Open Immunology 7(1):iqag010, received 2025-12-22, accepted 2026-06-05, published online 2026-06-13. Patient-Led Research Collaborative (Davis, Pollack, Cohen are prominent long-COVID patient-researchers). n=6,031, 162 symptoms, three clustering methods (cross-method agreement weak, adjusted mutual information 0.13-0.40). Methodological/epidemiological rather than biomedical mechanism, but bears directly on how phenotype/subtype papers already tracked should be interpreted. ~2.8 months old at time of recording — outside the tightest daily window but within the routine's 'roughly 3 months' allowance, and missed by prior runs (only now surfaced via Europe PMC's FIRST_PDATE indexing). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record and the Oxford Academic publisher page (full text fetched).

papers.title: Wearable-derived cardiopulmonary fitness and physical activity in adults with long COVID: a RECOVER-Adult digital health substudy
papers.authors: Vogel JM, Jenkins T, Cerda M, Chen H, Goldman J, Katz SD, et al., RECOVER Consortium
papers.summary: Using wrist-worn fitness trackers on almost 1,500 people an average of about 21 months after COVID-19, researchers found that those with a high long-COVID symptom burden had lower heart-rate variability at rest, a faster resting heart rate, and were far less physically active day-to-day than those with a low symptom burden — showing the fitness drop is real, measurable, and does not simply fade with time.
papers.why: Objectively confirms, with wearable data rather than just questionnaires, that long COVID can cause a lasting drop in heart and activity fitness nearly two years out, and raises the question of whether long COVID itself becomes a long-term heart-health risk factor.
papers.notes: JACC: Advances 5(7):102923, Jul 2026. Digital-health substudy of the NIH RECOVER-Adult cohort. n=1,475 (72% female). Associational, not causal (observational design). Overlaps with existing tracked PEM/autonomic-dysfunction and cardiopulmonary-exercise-testing entries but at much larger n via wearable data than typical CPET studies. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (full abstract fetched).

papers.title: Cognitive rehabilitation for adults with long COVID: a randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Vanova M, Patel AMR, Scott I, Gilpin G, Manning EN, Ash C, Wittenberg P, Lim J, Hoare Z, Evans R, Bray N, Kipps CM, Devine C, Ahmed S, Dunne R, Koniotes A, Warren C, Chan D, Suarez-Gonzalez A
papers.summary: In this England-based trial, 78 adults with lasting brain fog after COVID-19 were randomly given either ten weekly one-on-one 'cognitive rehabilitation' sessions (practical coaching on personally chosen everyday goals, like remembering appointments) or usual care. People who got the coaching made significantly more progress on their chosen goals than those on usual care, and much of the benefit was still there six months later.
papers.why: A well-designed randomized trial — a rarer and stronger type of evidence — showing a real, non-drug treatment can meaningfully help the brain-fog side of long COVID, a symptom with no approved treatment.
papers.notes: JAMA Network Open 9(7):e2620687, published 2026-07-01. NCT05731570. Multicenter (3 England sites), single-blind, n=78 randomized (38 CR / 40 usual care) of a planned 88. Primary outcome (goal-attainment, Bangor Goal-Setting Interview) at 3 months: adjusted mean difference 2.88 (95% CI 2.03-3.73, p<.001, Cohen's d=1.57), sustained but attenuated at 6 months (d=0.91). Non-drug/behavioral intervention — in scope for the papers track (not drug-restricted, unlike trials). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (full abstract with results fetched).

papers.title: Auditory sensory gating (P50 suppression) as a biomarker of cognitive fatigue in long COVID
papers.authors: Mischke M, Zaehle T
papers.summary: Researchers measured a specific brain-wave response called P50 suppression — how well the brain filters out repeated, unimportant sounds — in 71 people with long-COVID fatigue. People whose brains were worse at this filtering task reported more mental (cognitive) fatigue, even after accounting for depression.
papers.why: Points to a simple, objective brain-wave measurement that tracks brain-based fatigue independently of mood, which could help build a much-needed objective test for 'brain fog' in long COVID and ME/CFS.
papers.notes: Neuropsychology (APA), published online 2026-08-31. German group (T. Zaehle, Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg, neurology/cognitive neuroscience). n=71, cross-sectional, modest effect size (Kendall's tau=-.173, p=.037). Same P50-suppression marker previously studied in MS fatigue; first reported use in long COVID. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated (German group, but a papers-track entry — no German trial connection implied). Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (full abstract with results fetched).

papers.title: Nutraceuticals targeting mitochondrial and oxidative-inflammatory pathways for post-exertional malaise and cognitive impairment in long COVID: a narrative review
papers.authors: Praet SFE
papers.summary: This review pulls together existing research on cell energy production (mitochondria), harmful oxygen byproducts (oxidative stress), and inflammatory signalling molecules to propose that specific vitamins, minerals, and supplements ('nutraceuticals') acting on these pathways could help long-COVID post-exertional malaise (the crash after activity) and brain fog — though this is a proposed framework, not a tested treatment.
papers.why: Offers a structured, testable roadmap for future nutraceutical trials in long COVID/ME-CFS-type PEM, but it is a hypothesis-generating narrative review with no new patient data of its own, so treat it as a research agenda rather than evidence that a treatment works.
papers.notes: Nutrients 18(16):2650, published 2026-08-13; journal version of a 2026-07-14 Preprints.org preprint (DOI 10.20944/preprints202607.0899.v1) — distinct from the already-tracked, separately-sourced micronutrition review (DOI 10.3390/nu18162702, journal version of a different Preprints.org preprint 10.20944/preprints202607.1446.v1). Narrative/hypothesis review, no new primary data — borderline against the 'reviews with no new data' exclusion, included because it offers a specific, citable mechanistic framework rather than a general overview, same tier as other tracked hypothesis pieces. University of Canberra Research Institute for Sport and Exercise, Australia. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record and Crossref metadata (author affiliation, journal/volume/page).

papers.title: Prevalence and Functional Outcomes of Post-Exertional Malaise among Adults with prior COVID-19: Results from a Representative Survey of New York City Residents
papers.authors: Packard SE, et al.
papers.summary: A survey of over 9,600 New York City adults who previously had COVID-19 found that about one in five still gets post-exertional malaise (PEM) -- a crash after physical or mental effort -- and roughly 4% have symptoms lasting long enough to meet ME/CFS criteria.
papers.why: It's one of the largest population-representative estimates of how common PEM is after COVID-19, and shows it falls hardest on women, transgender/non-binary people, people of color, and people with less education or existing disabilities -- useful evidence for why clinics should screen for PEM routinely.
papers.notes: Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC/medRxiv preprint record (title, authors, DOI, posting date).

papers.title: Micronutrition as a Therapeutic Strategy for Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Fibromyalgia: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Abanades S, Fernandez I, Capdevila N, Cardona F
papers.summary: This review rounds up evidence that faulty cell energy production (mitochondrial dysfunction) and cell damage from unstable molecules (oxidative stress) contribute to ME/CFS and fibromyalgia, and asks whether nutrients like NAD+ boosters, B-vitamins, magnesium and CoQ10 could help.
papers.why: It's a plausible, low-risk treatment angle, but the authors themselves say solid trial evidence for these supplements in ME/CFS specifically is still thin and call for dedicated randomized trials.
papers.notes: Nutrients 18(16):2702, published 2026-08-19. This exact paper/DOI had not previously entered data/papers.json despite a 2026-09-02 CHANGELOG note describing it as 'already tracked' -- that note appears to have been mistaken (confused with the separately-authored, separately-DOI'd praet-2026-nutraceutical-bioenergetic-pem-review, Nutrients 18(16):2650, same issue). An earlier Preprints.org preprint version of this Abanades work (10.20944/preprints202607.1446.v1) was repeatedly and correctly screened out in prior runs for failing the credibility bar (not peer-reviewed); it now qualifies as peer-reviewed via this Nutrients publication. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC/journal record (authors, journal, volume/issue/article number, DOI).

papers.title: Beyond genes: EpiSwitch® and Orion platform-powered 3D genome architecture biomarkers reveal shared biology across ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis
papers.authors: Hunter E, Alshaker H, Vugrinec D, Bautista S, Gebregzabhar A, Virdi A, Croxford J, Dring A, Powell R, Salter M, Kingdon C, Green J, Akoulitchev A, Pchejetski D
papers.summary: Some genes are switched on or off depending on how DNA is folded up in 3D inside the cell, not just by the DNA code itself. Using a technology that reads this 3D folding pattern, researchers compared blood samples from people with ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis, and found overlapping folding-pattern "fingerprints" shared across these very different-looking illnesses.
papers.why: Suggests these conditions may share some deeper, measurable biology despite looking different on the surface, and extends the same group's earlier ME/CFS-specific biomarker work (EpiSwitch) into a cross-disease comparison that could eventually help with diagnosis.
papers.notes: J Transl Med, published online 2026-08-22. UK group (PhosphoBiomed/Oxford Biodynamics; Akoulitchev/Pchejetski senior authors) building on the group's earlier ME/CFS EpiSwitch chromosome-conformation biomarker work (already tracked as hunter-2025-episwitch-biomarker) with a new cross-disease comparison (ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, RA, MS) via the EpiSwitch/Orion 3D-genome-architecture platform. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Uncovering the hidden biology of fibrinaloid microclot complexes in complex, inflammatory diseases
papers.authors: Grixti J, Pretorius E, Kell DB
papers.summary: "Microclots" are unusually tough, hard-to-dissolve blood clots that some researchers think build up in inflammatory illnesses. This review by a leading microclot research group explains how these clots form, why the body struggles to break them down, and how they might cause symptoms in diseases including ME/CFS and long COVID.
papers.why: Consolidates and extends the microclot/endothelial (blood-vessel-lining) hypothesis that also motivates some ME/CFS and long-COVID treatment ideas, from the research group (Pretorius/Kell) most closely associated with this line of work.
papers.notes: QRB Discovery, published online 2026-07-31. Review article, no new patient data, by Pretorius/Kell (Stellenbosch/Liverpool), the group most associated with the fibrinaloid microclot hypothesis in long COVID/ME-CFS. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Low serum selenium combined with SELENOP-autoantibodies are associated with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection
papers.authors: Schmidt B, Asaad S, Mavarani L, Stang A, Chillon TS, Minich WB, Renko K, Brenner T, Schöler LM, Dittmer U, Trilling M, Schomburg L
papers.summary: Selenium is a mineral the body needs, and SELENOP is a blood protein that carries it around. In about 750 adults roughly two years after a COVID-19 infection, people with low selenium levels and antibodies that mistakenly attack SELENOP were more likely to still have fatigue — hinting that a mineral shortage, possibly made worse by the immune system attacking its carrier, might contribute to long-lasting tiredness.
papers.why: Points to a new, easily measurable biomarker (blood selenium plus SELENOP-autoantibodies) for post-viral fatigue and raises an obvious next question — whether selenium supplementation could help — that could be tested in a trial.
papers.notes: Redox Biology, published online 2026-06-27. German group (Essen University Hospital / University Duisburg-Essen). n~750, roughly 2 years post-SARS-CoV-2, cross-sectional biomarker association study (serum selenium, SELENOP levels and anti-SELENOP autoantibodies vs persistent fatigue). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Increased Mannosylation of Extracellular Vesicles in Long COVID Plasma as a Binding Target for Galanthus nivalis Agglutinin (GNA) Affinity Resin
papers.authors: Pesqueira Sanchez MA, de Necochea Campion R, Dalhuisen T, Fehrman EA, Chhabra PS, Kelly JD, Martin JN, Deeks SG, Henrich TJ, Peluso MJ, LaRosa SP
papers.summary: Cells release tiny particles into the blood called extracellular vesicles (EVs), a bit like sealed messages. In long-COVID patients, these EVs carry unusual sugar coatings on their surface. Researchers show a plant-derived sugar-binding material can selectively grab EVs with this coating out of blood — a step toward both a diagnostic test and a way to filter disease-linked particles out of the blood.
papers.why: From the well-known UCSF LIINC long-COVID research group; opens up both a new biomarker idea and a possible future blood-filtering (apheresis-like) treatment approach, similar in spirit to the immunoadsorption trials already tracked here.
papers.notes: IJMS 27(13):5723, published online 2026-06-25. UCSF LIINC long-COVID cohort (senior authors Deeks/Henrich/Peluso). Proof-of-concept EV surface-glycosylation (mannosylation) profiling and affinity-capture method. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Molecular, cellular and network mapping of brain structural deviations in patients with Post-COVID19 syndrome
papers.authors: Martins D, Cai Z, Mariani N, Borsini A, Mondelli V, Eiff B, Rota S, van Wamelen D, Nicholson T, Rida L, Hampshire A, Fernandes L, Zelaya F, Podlewska A, Chaudhuri R, Turkheimer F, Williams SCR, Veronese M
papers.summary: Brain scans of 20 people with ongoing tiredness after a mild COVID-19 infection showed subtle thickness changes in certain brain regions — especially areas rich in the same protein the coronavirus uses to enter cells, and areas involved in mood and the brain chemical serotonin.
papers.why: Gives direct brain-imaging evidence that fatigue can follow even a mild infection, and links it to specific, testable biology (viral-entry receptors, serotonin circuits) that could point to future drug targets.
papers.notes: Brain Behav Immun Health, published online 2026-06-26. King's College London group. n=20 persistent-fatigue-after-mild-COVID patients, structural MRI with molecular/receptor-density mapping (co-registered PET-derived atlases). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Pilot longitudinal integrated transcriptomic-metabolomic study reveals immune and metabolic signatures in non-hospitalized healthcare workers with long COVID
papers.authors: Espín E, Yang C, Shannon CP, Checkervarty AK, Kim S, Lapp L, Assadian S, Grunau B, Goldfarb DM, Hutton J, Huan T, Tebbutt SJ
papers.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
papers.summary: Healthcare workers who developed long COVID after a mild (non-hospitalized) infection, with fatigue and brain fog as their main symptoms, had unusual patterns in their immune-cell genes and blood chemistry compared to co-workers who fully recovered.
papers.why: Fills a gap in long-COVID biomarker research, which mostly studies people sick enough to be hospitalized — this looks at the milder, more ME/CFS-like presentation that is harder to study but affects far more people.
papers.notes: Front Cell Infect Microbiol, published online 2026-06-04. Canadian group (University of British Columbia / BC Children's Hospital). Small pilot, longitudinal transcriptomic + metabolomic profiling of non-hospitalized healthcare workers with long COVID (fatigue/brain-fog-predominant) vs recovered controls. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Small extracellular vesicles proteome reveals persistent inflammatory and coagulopathic dysregulation in long-COVID
papers.authors: Chandran S, Chen L, Ram AK, Spikes L, Chalise P, Dhillon NK
papers.summary: In long-COVID patients with fatigue, brain fog and sleep problems, the proteins carried by tiny blood particles called extracellular vesicles showed lasting signs of inflammation and abnormal blood-clotting activity.
papers.why: Adds another piece of evidence, via a different lab and method, for the inflammation-plus-abnormal-clotting picture in long COVID — the same "microclot" territory as other papers tracked here.
papers.notes: Front Immunol, published online 2026-07-20. US group (University of Kansas Medical Center). Small-EV proteomic profiling in long-COVID patients (fatigue/brain-fog/sleep-disturbance symptom profile) vs controls; inflammatory and coagulation-pathway protein dysregulation. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Associations between multidimensional fatigue and wearable-derived cardio-respiratory variables in post-COVID-19 patients: an observational study
papers.authors: Adão Martins NR, Annaheim S, Büche D, Rossi RM, Spengler CM
papers.summary: 30 people in post-COVID rehab wore sensors day and night that tracked their heart rate and breathing. Physical tiredness, mental tiredness, and emotional tiredness each lined up with a different pattern in these body signals.
papers.why: Supports using wrist- or chest-worn sensors as an objective way to track different kinds of fatigue over time — useful for helping patients pace themselves and for measuring whether future treatments actually help.
papers.notes: Front Digit Health, published online 2026-07-16. Swiss group (Empa / ETH Zurich). n=30 post-COVID rehabilitation patients, continuous wearable cardio-respiratory monitoring correlated with multidimensional fatigue questionnaire subscales (physical/mental/emotional). Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in Long COVID: prevalence and impact on health-related quality of life and health status. A cross-sectional study. BioICOPER study
papers.authors: Navarro-Cáceres A, Gómez-Sánchez L, Suárez-Moreno N, Arroyo-Romero S, Domínguez-Martín A, Lugones-Sánchez C, González-Sánchez S, Castro-Rivero AB, Gómez-Marcos MA, Navarro-Matías EN
papers.summary: Among 304 people with long COVID in Spain, a substantial subgroup met older, formal Chronic Fatigue Syndrome criteria. That subgroup had noticeably worse quality of life and overall health than the long-COVID patients who didn't meet those criteria.
papers.why: Puts a number on how large and how much worse-off the ME/CFS-like subgroup within long COVID is, which matters for how these patients are defined, studied, and prioritised for care and trials.
papers.notes: Research Square preprint, posted 2026-06-09, not yet peer-reviewed. Spanish group (BioICOPER study, Salamanca). n=304 long-COVID patients; cross-sectional comparison of those meeting Fukuda CFS criteria vs those who don't, on quality-of-life and health-status measures. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API preprint record (title/authors/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Symptom-based clusters in people with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC)
papers.authors: Kuczyk C, Herrmann-Lingen C, Stolz M, Krauth C, Burger B, Stahmeyer JT, Nöhre M, Debener A, Käufer C, Richter F, Derad C, Hellmich M, de Zwaan M
papers.summary: In 1,673 people with post-COVID condition in Germany, researchers grouped patients by their pattern of 14 symptoms (including fatigue) rather than by a single label, and found distinct subgroups that differed in age, sex, and psychological factors.
papers.why: A large German post-COVID cohort adds to the case that "post-COVID condition" isn't one single illness but several patient subgroups, which matters for tailoring treatment and for how future German trials define who to enroll.
papers.notes: J Transl Med, published online 2026-07-11. German group (Hannover Medical School / MHH, Herrmann-Lingen/de Zwaan). n=1,673 post-COVID-19 condition patients in Germany; symptom-based cluster analysis (14 symptoms incl. fatigue). Complements the already-tracked DecodeME/Habermann-Horstmeier subgrouping papers. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/journal/date/DOI match).

papers.title: Acute Protein Responses Control SARS-CoV-2-specific Neurocognitive and General Post-Viral Sequelae
papers.authors: Liou TG, Andrews RJ, Bass BL, et al. (33 authors, incl. Adler FR)
papers.summary: Researchers tested saliva samples taken soon after a COVID-19 infection and found that people whose bodies made more of certain antiviral immune proteins early on were less likely to develop lasting brain fog and fatigue-type symptoms months later.
papers.why: A simple, early saliva test might one day flag who is at risk of long-term post-viral fatigue and brain fog, and points to specific immune proteins as possible treatment targets.
papers.notes: medRxiv preprint, University of Utah group (Liou/Adler et al.), 33 authors. Saliva proteomics cohort linking acute-phase antiviral protein responses to reduced risk of later neurocognitive/general post-viral sequelae (fatigue, brain fog) after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record (title/authors/source/DOI exact match); direct medRxiv page fetch returned HTTP 403, so confirmation rests on Europe PMC's structured metadata record rather than the raw preprint page.

papers.title: Abnormal post-exercise depression of corticomotor excitability is associated with fatigue in post-COVID-19 condition
papers.authors: Sebastianelli L, Dezi S, Ortelli P, Ferrazzoli D, Oliviero A, Versace V
papers.summary: Using magnetic pulses to test brain-to-muscle signaling before and after exercise in 58 people with long COVID, researchers found the brain's motor output failed to recover normally after physical effort, and this abnormal pattern matched how fatigued patients said they felt.
papers.why: Gives doctors an objective, brain-based way to measure post-exertional fatigue instead of relying only on self-reported tiredness, which could help diagnose patients and track treatment response in future trials.
papers.notes: Clinical Neurophysiology (Elsevier), Italian group (Sebastianelli et al., Villa Beretta Rehabilitation Center / Vita-Salute San Raffaele). TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) study of post-exercise corticomotor excitability in 58 post-COVID-19 patients with fatigue as the primary outcome. Not Wirth/Scheibenbogen-affiliated. Confirmed via Europe PMC REST API record and DOI resolution to the Clinical Neurophysiology/ScienceDirect page (PII S1388245726008849).
